papers.title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
papers.authors: Yong Hwi Song, Keon Myung Lee
papers.abstract: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.

papers.title: HolidayFactory 1.0: Simulating, Generating, and Evaluating Industrial Robot Tasks
papers.authors: Holiday Robotics, :, Jeongmin Lee, Taehyeon Kim, Dohyun Jang, Minji Lee, Seonghun Oh, Dongwoo Park, et al.
papers.abstract: Robots are typically evaluated in episodes that begin from a reset, while industrial work consists of repeated jobs whose outcomes affect subsequent operations. Evaluating such work at scale requires simulation of task-critical physical interactions, construction of industrial environments, and measurements of performance as scene state persists. We present HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0, a framework for simulating, generating, and evaluating industrial robot work. Given a human-specified workplace and task, the framework defines a world pairing a scenario of scene variants and process logic with an evaluation defining a job, metrics, and a rubric. HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0 comprises three components. HOLIDAY-SIM extends Newton's SDF-based hydroelastic contact with additional constitutive laws and a semi-implicit primal-dual solver, couples stateful actuator dynamics to articulated motion, and derives tactile and joint observations from simulated states. Agentic world construction generates simulation-ready assets and scene variants using geometric and interaction checks, and proposes task-conditioned evaluations for human confirmation and executable checks. 24/7-BENCH introduces seven industrial tasks in which jobs are evaluated without resetting the scene, measuring completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy. Controlled studies characterize the proposed contact, actuator, and tactile models and examine the effectiveness of verification-guided world construction. Experiments on scene and evaluation generation further reveal the limitations of model critics and the difficulty of ensuring that generated evaluations faithfully capture task requirements. We examine job-level evaluations with scripted trajectories (e.g., code-as-policy) but have not yet compared policies over persistent runs.

papers.title: Hierarchical Multi-Channel Tip-Over Prediction via Isolated Temporal Models for Planetary Rover Safety
papers.authors: Siddhant Shete, Raul Dominguez, Frank Kirchner
papers.abstract: Reliable tip-over prevention is critical for planetary rovers operating in unstructured environments where communication delays prevent real-time human intervention. Existing learning-based approaches typically optimize a single prediction objective, limiting their ability to capture both gradual instability evolution and abrupt terrain disturbances. This work presents a hierarchical multi-channel tip-over prediction framework based on isolated temporal learning. A multi-horizon Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) learns progressive instability patterns from inertial measurements, while a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based forward dynamics model predicts nominal rover motion and detects unexpected dynamic deviations through prediction residuals. These complementary signals are integrated through decision-level fusion and priority-based arbitration to generate graded safety actions, including early warning and emergency braking. The proposed system is deployed as an Orocos Real-Time Toolkit (RTT)-based safety component within the Rock robotics framework, operating at 100 Hz on a planetary rover software stack. Experiments on Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) samples collected across heterogeneous terrains demonstrate 97.58% event prediction coverage with a 1.82s median lead time, outperforming individual prediction channels. The results validate that isolated temporal models combined through hierarchical decision fusion provide a robust solution for real-time rover safety in uncertain terrain.

papers.title: Hardware-Rooted Neural AI Safety, Influence Verification, and Execution-Finality Control for European Sovereign AI, Frontier Models, and Critical Infrastructure
papers.authors: Sangam Das
papers.abstract: TECHNICAL DISCLOSURE — EUROPEAN AI SAFETY AND SOVEREIGN AI INFRASTRUCTURE Technical Subtitle: Protected Neural Provenance, Autonomous Agent Execution, GPU Inference, Data Sovereignty, and Cryptographic Authorization of Consequential AI Actions Abstract What happens when an autonomous AI model generates an action that its safety guardrails, access controls, or runtime policies fail to prevent? As frontier neural networks evolve from generating information toward autonomous reasoning, coding, tool execution, persistent memory, multimodal perception, and real-world operations, a fundamental safety challenge emerges: whether a neural-generated output should possess the technical authority to become an externally effective consequence. This challenge is increasingly relevant to Europe's development of trustworthy artificial intelligence, sovereign computing infrastructure, industrial AI, critical information systems, and high-assurance autonomous technologies. This technical disclosure presents a proposed hardware-rooted neural-AI execution-finality architecture, published under International Patent Application PCT/IB2026/056809 (WO/2026/172334 A2), for governing consequential operations generated by frontier foundation models, autonomous agents, distributed neural networks, and AI-enabled critical infrastructure. The disclosed architecture introduces Neural Candidate Acts, Neural State Descriptors, Neural Trust Segments, Neural Influence Maps, Multimodal Sensory Provenance Seals, and Hardware-Isolated Shadow Auditors to support protected evaluation of model identity, instruction provenance, untrusted-context influence, runtime behavior, and authorized operational conditions. Generated tokens, tool calls, shell commands, persistent-memory updates, database writes, data exports, payment instructions, GPU-generated outputs, and other consequential operations may be maintained in a structurally non-effective state until a Protected Enforcement Domain validates applicable execution predicates, commits cryptographically protected validation evidence, and releases scoped, non-bearer execution authority. An independent Finality Sink subsequently verifies that authority at the relevant effectuation boundary before permitting the operation to become effective. The proposed two-boundary mechanism distinguishes AI computation, policy permission, and model-output generation from the protected authority necessary for actual execution. Additional embodiments address prompt-injection influence, poisoned retrieval, unauthorized neural-context manipulation, persistent-memory contamination, speculative decoding, model and adapter substitution, distributed GPU computation, cross-jurisdictional data export, covert intelligence-related data transmission, satellite communications, telecommunications infrastructure, financial settlement, and autonomous cyber-physical operations. European AI Act, Digital Sovereignty, and Trustworthy AI Relevance The architecture is potentially relevant to the European Union's objectives concerning trustworthy AI, technological sovereignty, privacy-preserving computing, resilience, and responsible deployment of increasingly autonomous systems. Its protected execution evidence, neural-runtime validation, authorization freshness, and independent finality verification may support technical risk-management activities associated with the EU AI Act, including requirements concerning record-keeping under Article 12, human oversight under Article 14, and accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity under Article 15, where these provisions apply. The proposed separation between access to personal or enterprise data and authorization for consequential data export may also complement the GDPR's data-protection-by-design principles, including Article 25, and support technical approaches to jurisdiction-aware processing, data minimization, and controlled cross-border transmission. For European operators of regulated and essential services, the architecture may also be relevant to cybersecurity and operational-resilience objectives associated with NIS2 and the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), depending on the deployment context. These potential technical contributions do not themselves establish compliance with any European regulation. European AI Models and Industrial Technology Alignment The proposed architecture has potential applicability to European AI development environments, including Mistral AI's Mistral Large and other foundation models, Vibe autonomous productivity and coding agents, and Mistral AI Studio; Aleph Alpha's PhariaAI sovereign enterprise AI platform; SAP Business AI and Joule; and European sovereign-cloud and confidential-computing infrastructure. For these environments, potential integrations include protected authorization of autonomous tool calls, verification of permitted model and runtime states, controlled release of neural outputs, governance of persistent AI memory, and restrictions on unauthorized data export. European AI developers and infrastructure providers could investigate implementing the architecture without replacing their existing foundation models or application frameworks, provided suitable protected-validation components and enforceable execution endpoints are available. The same architectural principles may be relevant to global AI ecosystems, including Anthropic Claude and Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Agents SDK, Google Gemini and Gemini Enterprise, Microsoft Copilot Studio and Agent 365, and NVIDIA AI inference and confidential-computing platforms. Potential integration would complement existing model alignment, safety guardrails, identity management, runtime isolation, agent observability, and application permissions with protected neural-state-aware authorization and independent verification before consequential execution. Industrial Significance for Europe The principal industrial opportunity is a reusable, model-independent execution-authority infrastructure for increasingly capable AI systems. Potential applications include sovereign enterprise AI, autonomous software engineering, privacy-sensitive cloud inference, industrial robotics, telecommunications, financial transactions, critical infrastructure, and public-sector AI services. The architecture may help European developers and infrastructure operators separate innovation in neural-model capabilities from security-critical decisions over execution, data movement, and physical or financial consequences. Neural influence analysis remains technically challenging, and cryptographic validation of an attribution record does not independently establish that the record correctly explains a model's internal causal behavior. Consequently, practical integration requires suitable runtime instrumentation, reliable validation methods, enforceable effectuation boundaries, and independent experimental assessment. Core Technical Principle: AI may compute, reason, predict, learn, and propose—but computation alone must not confer authority to act. The disclosure presents a potential technical foundation for European sovereign AI, trustworthy autonomous systems, and security-conscious frontier-model deployment while preserving the distinction between proposed architecture, demonstrated technical performance, and regulatory compliance. papers.title: Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control for Underactuated Upright Physical Assistance
papers.authors: Darren Biskup, Jeonghan Yu, Zibo Yu, Sunil K. Agrawal
papers.abstract: Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user's instantaneous human-ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance. By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon. We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants. Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area. The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human-ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators.

papers.title: Grasping the Future: Joint 3D Hand-Object Forecasting From Internet Videos
papers.authors: Rustin Soraki, Matthew Wallingford, Ryan Aby, Brandon Chee, Jason Ren, Ali Farhadi, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Roozbeh Mottaghi
papers.abstract: To interact with an object, we need to anticipate both how it will move and how our hands should move with it. Human videos capture these relationships across everyday activities, offering a natural source for learning to predict future interactions. Learning from them requires recovering motion from completed interactions and using it to anticipate what could happen next. We present $\textit{Grasping-the-Future}$, a unified generative model of joint 3D hand-object motion, including wrist motion, finger articulation, and object position and orientation. Through masked spatiotemporal completion and flow matching, we train a single model for several prediction tasks: forecasting future interactions, predicting hand motion given object motion or vice versa, generating both trajectories toward a desired final object pose, and completing partially observed interactions. We explicitly model hand-object relations and incorporate contact constraints to help preserve grasp relationships during motion. To obtain 3D supervision from internet videos, we develop a scalable pipeline that combines pretrained perception models with joint geometric optimization to reconstruct completed interactions. We combine these recovered trajectories with annotated interaction datasets as training data for all tasks. We demonstrate strong performance across all tasks, outperforming released forecasters on datasets with 3D annotations. Moreover, we show geometric and physical plausibility of the predicted trajectories by retargeting them to a robotic embodiment. Videos are available at https://grasping-the-future.github.io.

papers.title: Grasp-Taxonomy Conditioning as a Mode Switch for Dexterous Grasping of Climbing Holds
papers.authors: Rumi Loghmani, Abraham George, Amir Barati Farimani
papers.abstract: Dexterous grasping in robotics relies on distinct hand configurations depending on object geometry. We introduce BetaGrasp, a 3D diffusion policy that conditions a DP3-style point-cloud policy on a four-class grasp label (crimp, sloper, pinch, and jug), running on a Franka arm with a 16-DoF LEAP hand. We also introduce a climbing-hold benchmark: a spring testbed whose ratchet gives a slip-force reading in newtons. In our analysis the policy's point-cloud encoder did not separate the four holds, so the scan alone gave it little to choose a grasp from. Without the label (a DP3-style baseline), simulated rollouts from the robot's reset pose all end in a jug grasp, whatever the hold (25% correct grasp type, versus 94% for BetaGrasp). The label works as a switch for which grasp the policy performs. On 80 paired hardware trials, BetaGrasp raises average slip force from 9.6 N to 14.3 N, and grasps slipping fully off the hold drop from 44% of trials to 10%.

papers.title: Graph-Sparse Distributed Predictive Control for Multi-Robot Motion Planning vianEdge-Consensus ADMM
papers.authors: Josep Borras-Borras, Pablo Segovia, Carlos Ocampo-Martinez
papers.abstract: This paper presents a distributed model predictive control (MPC) architecture for collision-avoiding motion planning of planar robots with double-integrator dynamics. To reduce coordination demands, a time-varying predicted conflict graph selects relevant pairwise interactions. The associated collision-avoidance constraints are convexified once per MPC update using warm-start trajectories, yielding a fixed convex quadratic program (QP). The resulting QP is then decomposed using an edge-consensus formulation of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), enabling parallel robot-local optimization and independent closed-form projections onto separating half-spaces. Execution is selectively supervised by a centralized high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) QP when the distributed candidate does not satisfy the direct-execution conditions. Evaluated in C++ simulations involving 8, 16, and 32 robots, the proposed architecture achieves collision-free execution and substantially improves computational scalability while maintaining task-level performance comparable to a centralized complete-graph baseline.

papers.title: GeoMind: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Jinghe Wang, Xinrui Cao, Duo Wu, Chenghao Gu, Yong Zhong, Linjia Kang, Tianyi Xiong, Zhi Wang
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.

papers.title: Generative AI chatbots and mental health: A critical narrative review of benefits, risks, and clinical implications
papers.authors: Bruno da Silva Santos, Arthur Dolberth, Giovanni Gonçalves De Toni, Carlos Eduardo Freitas Dantas, Matheus de Lima Ruffini, Flávio Pereira Kapczinski, Jaime E. C. Hallak, Ives Cavalcante Passos
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence chatbots has repositioned these systems from productivity tools to interlocutors used for emotional support, companionship, and mental health guidance. This critical narrative review has three aims: to give mental health professionals a concise technical account of large language models; to separate the evidence and risks attached to four distinct system classes, protocolized therapeutic chatbots, clinically bounded generative systems, general-purpose large language models used as informal therapy, and companion platforms; and to examine clinical, ethical, and regulatory implications. Literature was identified through non-systematic, iterative database and preprint-server searches between March and July 2026, supplemented by citation tracking and policy documents. No prespecified eligibility or screening protocol was used; the comparative claims are therefore provisional. Protocolized and clinically bounded systems carry the strongest evidence, including a meta-analysis of generative and hybrid chatbots reporting modest short-term symptom reduction and a randomized trial of an expert-fine-tuned therapeutic chatbot; these trials are brief, predominantly waitlist-controlled, and reliant on self-report. General-purpose models and companion platforms may deliver immediate validation and temporary reductions in loneliness, but that evidence is largely observational, qualitative, or short-term experimental and does not establish sustained benefit. Concerns include emotional dependence, social substitution, sycophantic reinforcement, unsafe responses to suicidal or psychotic content, commercial manipulation, and delusional beliefs temporally associated with sustained use. These systems are not a single intervention class. Their effects appear contingent on clinical structure, relational design, user vulnerability, duration and centrality of use, commercial incentives, and safeguards.

papers.title: Galilean Robots, Aristotelian Sensors: Joint Spatiotemporal Trajectory Estimation and Extrinsic Calibration
papers.authors: Abhishek Goudar, Jonathan Kelly, Timothy D. Barfoot
papers.abstract: Multi-sensor state estimation requires accurate spatial and temporal calibration between heterogeneous sensors. Existing spatiotemporal calibration methods typically represent sensor extrinsic parameters as a rigid-body transformation together with a scalar temporal offset, causing the spatial and temporal parameters to enter the estimation problem through separate mechanisms. While the spatial transformation composes directly with the robot pose, accounting for the temporal offset requires evaluating the trajectory at a shifted time, typically through motion compensation, interpolation, or a continuous-time trajectory representation. In this work, we formulate joint trajectory estimation and spatiotemporal calibration using the special Galilean group for the robot trajectory and the Aristotelian subgroup for sensor extrinsics. This representation incorporates the coupling between motion and temporal offset directly through the group structure, avoiding the need for a separately parameterized continuous-time trajectory. We develop twist- and IMU-driven motion priors, accommodate both ideal and non-ideal clocks, and evaluate the framework with camera, position, and range measurements. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate calibration and trajectory-estimation performance comparable to established methods across heterogeneous sensor configurations. Our simplified framework therefore offers a quality-of-life improvement over existing methods without compromising performance.

papers.title: GAP: Generalized Adaptation Prior for Dexterous Piano Playing
papers.authors: Jinyi Chen, Hongyi Li, Lei Jiang, Xianwei Liu, Yanhong Liang, Yulin Chen, Yucheng Tao, Yongbin Jin, et al.
papers.abstract: Dexterous hands enable versatile manipulation, but policies trained in simulation often degrade on hardware owing to non-idealities, and the high-dimensional action space makes real-world adaptation costly. Piano playing, which requires precise and coordinated multifinger motion, offers a representative testbed. We propose GAP (Generalized Adaptation Prior for Dexterous Piano Playing), a sample-efficient adaptation framework that learns how to adapt, rather than how to act, during simulation pretraining and transfers this adaptation prior to hardware. Between repeated executions, GAP uses feedback to adjust the actions of the next one: a gradient guidance network learns from paired executions how adjusting actions affects playing performance, and its gradients guide these adjustments. In simulation, GAP yields approximately 2.4 times the F1 scores improvement of the existing fast-adaptation baseline for dexterous piano playing under the same interaction budget. The learned prior also generalizes to musical pieces held out from pretraining. On a physical dexterous hand, the same simulation-pretrained prior improves F1 scores by 3.6%-23% across three pieces of varying difficulty after approximately 7 min of adaptation each. These results suggest a practical route to reduce the real-world interaction needed to deploy dexterous hands.

papers.title: Force-Closure Condition for Cooperative Multi-robot Pushing of Rectangular Objects
papers.authors: Duy Anh Nguyen, Trung Dung Ngo
papers.abstract: In cooperative object manipulation, the placement of pushing contacts determines whether force closure can be achieved and agents can generate arbitrary forces and torques on the object correspondingly. This study derives a necessary and sufficient closed-form condition for the planar force closure of a rectangular object, a common object shape in everyday settings, under four frictionless pushing contacts. For a rectangle of length $b$ and width $a$, force closure holds if and only if $(l_1+l_3-b)(l_2+l_4-a)<0$, where $l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4$ are the four edge contact locations. This condition is independent of the object's center of mass and is used to verify contact configurations before contact force allocation. When the condition is not satisfied, the signs of the two factors indicate which opposing contact pair should be adjusted. The condition and adjustment rule are then integrated into a full-pose trajectory-tracking framework as a geometric feasibility layer to demonstrate their use in control. Static wrench feasibility tests validate the proposed condition, while narrow-passage floating-body simulations show that maintaining a force-closure configuration reduces the RMS tracking errors in $x$, $y$, and unwrapped yaw from $12.05$ m, $18.11$ m, and $535.96^\circ$ to $2.24$ m, $2.66$ m, and $2.69^\circ$, respectively.

papers.title: Flip Anything with Agentic Robotics Self-Learning
papers.authors: Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Ken Goldberg
papers.abstract: Flipping is a fundamental robotic manipulation skill that requires reorienting a target object in a stable pose on a planar support surface by rotating it 180$^\circ$ about an axis parallel to the support surface -- think of flipping a coin from heads to tails. Although flipping is a common objective in industrial tasks such as parts inspection, mechanical assembly, and tool use, coding a bimanual robot with grippers to flip diverse objects is a significant challenge. In this paper, we show that a coding agent can autonomously develop and refine object-flipping strategies through iterative learning in physics simulations across diverse object geometries. Progressive skill acquisition, from basic handover to toppling and pushing, robust grasping and sensing, and thin-object manipulation with recovery, improves task success from 24.7% to 95.0%. The resulting graph-based code integrates high-level strategy selection with reactive control, enabling multi-stage flipping on physical robots.

papers.title: False Prophets: On the Security of World Models in Agentic Systems
papers.authors: Erik Imgrund, Anna Wimbauer, Klim Kireev, Konrad Rieck
papers.abstract: Large language models now power autonomous agents capable of complex, multi-step tasks in different environments. Accurate and reliable execution of these tasks requires the agent to predict the results of its actions. Recent research proposes to enhance predictive capabilities via specially trained environment simulators—world models. While world models can improve performance, they can also mislead agents into executing harmful actions, creating significant security and privacy risks. In this paper, we raise security concerns regarding the usage of world models in agentic systems. We discover a range of world model specific vulnerabilities, which can be exploited in terminal-based agents to execute malicious code or extract sensitive data. To facilitate future development, we introduce a security benchmark dataset designed for text-based world models. We argue that some risks are intrinsic to approximate world modeling, and show that attackers can induce mispredictions in agentic pipelines with up to 95 % success rate, possibly resulting in unintended command execution, denial of service, drainage of wallet and private information extraction. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for practitioners to mitigate the discovered harms and harden agentic systems.

papers.title: Fade to... Red? Scheduling Coloured Noise Exploration Supports Efficient Robot Learning with Reduced Movement Jerk
papers.authors: Francisco M. López, Francisco Cruz
papers.abstract: Exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control is commonly driven by temporally uncorrelated Gaussian (white) action noise, which leads to jerky motions with locally constrained exploration. In contrast, temporally correlated coloured noise, particularly pink noise, has been shown to support more efficient exploration in RL. Motivated by these findings, we inquire whether scheduling changes to the noise colour over the course of training can outperform white noise for continuous control robotics. We perform a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, together with generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks with a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand. We find that the noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or end performance, whereas fading towards red noise halves the jerk of exploration in every task. Balancing learning efficiency, end performance and smoothness, red noise emerges as the preferred strategy: it learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less movement jerk. We therefore recommend exploration schedulers that fade towards red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.

papers.title: ExoStack: A Modular and Reconfigurable Software Framework for Wearable Robotics Using ROS 2
papers.authors: Debadrata Sarkar, Upamanyu Ray, Soumen Sen, Aman Arora
papers.abstract: Wearable robots depend on a software chain that links body-worn sensing to gait interpretation, assistance generation, and actuation. Personalization further requires each measured response to remain associated with the assistance parameters that generated it. This paper presents ExoStack, a modular ROS 2 framework for implementing that chain across embedded hubs and a host computer. Its Embedded Sensing and Actuation (ESA) library configures ESP32 boards as microROS sensing and actuation hubs. ExoCore supplies multi-hub synchronization, gait-event detection, profile generation, motion planning, cost evaluation, and human-in-the-loop (HIL) optimization as configuration-instantiated nodes. The PASE desktop application edits configurations, launches the processing stages, and visualizes ROS 2 topics. Hardware drivers and algorithm plugins can be added through defined interfaces without modifying the generic processing nodes. We characterize hub and planner timing on three embedded computers and demonstrate reuse on two pneumatic exosuits.

papers.title: Empowering Internet of Vehicles with Embodied Intelligence: A Survey of Technologies, Evaluation, and Outlook
papers.authors: Qiang Yu, Kebing Jin, Jianhang Tang, Xuanyu Wu, Yang Zhang, Celimuge Wu, Yixiong Feng
papers.abstract: Abstract The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) advances intelligent transportation by allowing vehicles, roadside infrastructure, pedestrian devices, and edge and cloud resources to share observations, computing resources, and traffic information. However, the traditional IoV systems often process perception, scene understanding, driving decisions, and vehicle control sequentially without continuously using feedback from vehicle motion execution to update later understanding and decisions, allowing state estimation and decision errors to persist across driving cycles and resulting in outdated vehicle states, decisions inconsistent with traffic conditions, and infeasible or unsafe maneuvers. Embodied intelligence forms a closed-loop in which vehicles perceive traffic conditions, understand scene changes, make decisions, execute control actions, and use environmental feedback to update later perception and decisions. This closed-loop reduces error accumulation, aligns traffic understanding with current road conditions, and improves vehicle action feasibility and adaptability. Existing surveys have reviewed embodied intelligence and related autonomous driving technologies. However, the closed-loop relationships among vehicle-to-everything (V2X) observations, traffic understanding, driving decision-making, vehicle execution, and environmental feedback have not been systematically examined. This survey organizes relevant studies around intelligent vehicle perception, traffic scene understanding, driving policy generation, and vehicle motion control, and clarifies the closed-loop process in which vehicles integrate multi-source observations collected by sensors to understand the current traffic scene, generate driving policies, control vehicle motion, and incorporate vehicle motion feedback into the next cycle of perception and decision making. The survey also summarizes representative datasets, metrics, challenges, and future directions for connected vehicles.

papers.title: Embodied First Exam
papers.authors: Kangrui Wang, Qineng Wang, Changhe Chen, Pingyue Zhang, Chi Gui, Feishi Wang, Canyu Chen, Wenli Xiao, et al.
papers.abstract: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.

papers.title: Effects of observing a robot expressing approach-avoidance conflict on observers’ self-evaluations of personal courage
papers.authors: Yuki Shimizu, Midori Ban, Hideyuki Takahashi, Hiroshi Ishiguro
papers.abstract: Courage involves pursuing a valued action despite fear, hesitation, or competing motives. However, the pre-action conflict relevant to judging an act as courageous is difficult to observe directly and manipulate systematically when another human serves as the model. Robots provide a means of representing such otherwise covert motives in a controlled and reproducible form. We therefore examined how a robot’s expression of approach-avoidance conflict is perceived and how it relates to observers’ immediate self-evaluations of personal courage. Speech bubbles were projected near the head of a cylindrical robot to present approach and avoidance motives in a scenario in which the robot encountered a person littering in a park. Study 1 compared conflict and no-conflict conditions and sequential and simultaneous presentation methods to determine whether a robot expressing approach-avoidance conflict was perceived as courageous. Study 2 varied whether the robot expressed one motive direction or both approach and avoidance motives and whether it admonished the litterer, and examined whether post-stimulus courage self-evaluations differed according to observers’ preexisting courage tendency. In Study 1, the conflict condition yielded higher courage and conflict ratings than the no-conflict condition. In Study 2, the predicted three-way interaction was not supported. Instead, we observed an interaction between preexisting courage tendency group and conflict expression that was not specified in the primary hypothesis, with self-evaluations in the conflict condition tending to be higher in the low-courage group and lower in the high-courage group. Although neither group’s conflict contrast was significant after correction for multiple comparisons, this contrasting pattern is an exploratory finding suggesting that robot-expressed conflict may be received differently depending on observers’ preexisting courage tendency. The study provides a controlled HRI paradigm for examining how robot-expressed motives are perceived and raises the possibility that user characteristics may be relevant when designing robots that display cues to internal processes.

papers.title: Echoes of Intelligence: What AI Could Learn From Bats
papers.authors: Rolf Müller
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid progress of deep learning has been driven in part by general principles of biological information processing, yet current AI systems still fall short of biological intelligence in critical ways such as integration of the computational and physical domains, i.e., embodied AI, and achieving autonomy in complex environments. This perspective argues that bat biosonar offers a particularly valuable model system for advancing embodied AI and autonomy in complex environments beyond the currently dominating vision‐centered and data‐intensive paradigms. Bats navigate dense and dynamic environments based on sparse trains of clutter echoes with random waveforms. These capabilities suggest alternative computational principles for perception and action: exploiting statistical rather than deterministic signal structure, extracting task‐relevant information from low‐bandwidth streams, and integrating morphology, actuation, and neural processing into closed‐loop embodied intelligence. This perspective reviews how bat biosonar differs from engineered sonar, identifies desirable capabilities that could inspire next‐generation autonomous systems, and outlines future research directions for deciphering and reproducing bat‐like intelligence through multimodal biological data, machine learning, neuromorphic processing, and biomimetic robotic platforms. By framing bat biosonar as a model for dynamic embodied intelligence, this perspective highlights a path toward AI systems that are more robust, parsimonious, and highly capable in real‐world environments.

papers.title: DreamLander: A 6-DOF World Model based Reinforcement Learning Planetary Lander
papers.authors: George Nehma, Patrick Quinn, Madhur Tiwari, Camilo Riano-Rios
papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.

papers.title: Does Total Knowledge Mute Emotion? A Thought Experiment using Large Language Models
papers.authors: M. Z. Naser
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether comprehensive knowledge acquisition attenuates emotional experience through a thought experiment that uses large language models (LLMs). We propose that LLMs, which possess extensive propositional knowledge yet lack phenomenal consciousness, serve as philosophical instruments for isolating the knowledge variable from other cognitive attributes. Our analysis develops two competing theoretical frameworks: the epistemic saturation hypothesis (ESH), which predicts emotional dampening via reduced prediction error, and the information hazard hypothesis (IHH), which anticipates emotional intensification via heightened awareness of negative states. We introduce a value uncertainty matrix that maps entities along the dimensions of knowledge completeness and embodied value schemas, thereby positioning hypothetical total knowledge agents (TKAs), LLMs, and humans within this conceptual space. Our synthesis suggests that total knowledge transforms rather than eliminates emotion and, therefore, shifts affective experience from uncertainty-driven volatility toward knowledge-dependent sublime states. This thought experiment reveals three insights: (1) vast propositional knowledge alone generates no intrinsic valence; (2) emotional experience requires embodied value computation; and (3) human cognitive enhancement toward total knowledge would likely preserve complex emotions while attenuating basic reactive effects. In parallel, the same thought experiment demonstrates how computational systems lacking consciousness can shed some light on fundamental questions about knowledge, emotion, and the nature of human experience.

papers.title: Does Haptic Connection to a Healthy Partner Improve Motor Learning in Chronic Stroke? A Pilot Study of Robot-Based Dyadic Training
papers.authors: Erica L. Waters, Natalia Stroutinsky-Sobotka, Reem M. Azar, Frances S. Shofer, Pamela Z. Cacchione, Rochelle J. Mendonca, Michelle J. Johnson
papers.abstract: Purpose: Robot-based haptic dyads, where two users exchange forces through robots, have been proposed for robot-assisted neurorehabilitation. This intervention could increase motor learning by promoting motor variability, providing an implicit communication channel, and facilitating social interaction. Despite the potential benefits, few studies have investigated robot-based haptic dyads for neurological populations, and none have included a comprehensive clinical assessment. Design/Methodology/Approach: We present a pilot study investigation of individuals with chronic stroke learning a complex tracking task in solo and dyad conditions. Prior to training, participants completed a battery of cognitive, motor, and sensory assessments. We assessed changes in key kinematic outcomes including tracking error, distance traveled, mean absolute power, and sample entropy. We also performed a correlation analysis of clinical scores with baseline tracking errors. Findings: Baseline tracking error was strongly correlated (r > 0.6) with lower cognitive scores and higher motor scores. Only the solo group demonstrated lower tracking error at assessment (Δ = -5.33, 95%CI [-10.25, -0.40], p = 0.027), but this result was tempered by the removal of an outlier participant. Neither group demonstrated clear retention. The dyad group showed significantly elevated performance, effort, and movement complexity during training. Research Limitations/Implications: The selected task was too difficult to reveal learning for either group, which may be related to its high cognitive demand. Sample size and stroke heterogeneity were also limitation. Originality/Value: Dyadic training increased movement complexity and effort, which are associated with better motor learning. Clinical characteristics such as lesion location, cognition, sensation, and chronicity may influence potential benefits of dyadic training.

papers.title: Distilling Instructions into Weights: Closed-Form Edits Fix a Robot Policy's Misreading
papers.authors: Ali-Adeeb Abbas, Esmaeil Seraj
papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.

papers.title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation
papers.authors: Haejoon Lee, Thomas Marshall Vielmetti, Xinyi Wang, Dimitra Panagou
papers.abstract: Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.

papers.title: DiffPhD: A Unified Differentiable Solver for Projective Heterogeneous Materials in Elastodynamics with Contact-Rich GPU-Acceleration
papers.authors: Shih-Yu Lai, Sung-Han Tien, Huang Jui-I, Y.H. Tseng, Yi-Ting Chiu, Siyuan Luo, Ziqiu Zeng, Fan Shi
papers.abstract: Differentiable simulation of soft bodies is a foundation for system identification, trajectory optimization, and Real2Sim transfer. Yet, existing methods such as the differentiable Projective Dynamics (DiffPD) struggle when faced with heterogeneous materials with extreme stiffness contrasts, hyperelasticity under large deformations, and contact-rich interactions, which are common scenarios in the real world. We present DiffPhD, a unified GPU-accelerated differentiable Projective Dynamics framework for heterogeneous materials that tackles these intertwined challenges simultaneously. Our key insight is a careful integration of: (i) stiffness-aware projective weights to embed heterogeneity into the global system; (ii) trust-region eigenvalue filtering lifted to the backward pass for stable hyperelastic gradients and a type-II Anderson Acceleration scheme with dual-gate convergence to stabilize forward iteration under large stiffness contrasts; and (iii) a unified GPU pipeline that reuses a single sparse factor across forward, backward, and contact computations, with stiffness-amplified Rayleigh damping folded into the same factor for heterogeneity-aware dissipation at zero recurring cost. DiffPhD delivers analytic adjoints—machine-precision on the elastic path, bounded and quantified under contact—with up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over prior differentiable solvers. Crucially, this speedup does not come at the cost of stability: DiffPhD remains convergent on stiffness contrasts up to 100× where prior PD solvers degrade. This unlocks end-to-end gradient-based optimization on regimes previously bottlenecked by either solver fragility or per-iteration cost—shell-joint composite creatures, soft characters wielding stiff weapons, and soft-gripper robotic manipulation—all handled within a single forward-backward pass. papers.title: Design of a hybrid tendon-linkage finger with coupled and adaptive motion
papers.authors: Hyojae Kang, Giup Seo, Jae-Young Lee, Yeong Jae Park, Jongwoo Park, Hyunmin Do, So-Hee Park, Dongil Park, et al.
papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic fingers require coordinated joint motion and adaptability to object contact, while independently actuating multiple joints increases the complexity of the transmission mechanism. This paper presents a hybrid tendon--linkage robotic finger with four mechanical degrees of freedom driven by three actuators. The MCP abduction/adduction joint is driven through a bevel gear, while MCP and PIP flexion/extension are driven by separate bidirectional tendon transmissions. The DIP joint is not independently actuated but is coupled to the PIP joint through a four-bar linkage with a torsional spring and mechanical stopper. The tendon routing also introduces mechanical coupling between the MCP and PIP joints. Kinematic analysis was conducted to describe the coupled and adaptive motions, and experiments were performed to evaluate the joint motion characteristics. ArUco-based measurements showed that the coupled motion closely matched the theoretical prediction, whereas the adaptive motion was partially limited by interference between linkage components. The fabricated finger demonstrated different contact postures with cylindrical, cuboid, and irregularly shaped objects, and the mean peak fingertip force was 4.56 N. The proposed mechanism provides both coupled motion and contact-dependent adaptation without requiring an additional actuator for the DIP joint.

papers.title: DeltaForge: A Post-hoc Mixture-of-Experts VLA for Multi-Domain Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Bingzhang Wang, Mo Poorsartep, Yasaman Esfandiari
papers.abstract: Fleets of driving vision-language-action (VLA) models are developed one domain at a time: each operator finetunes a shared base model on private data, producing specialized experts that are costly to consolidate into a single model. Weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate, and dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive to combine them. We present DeltaForge, to our knowledge the first post-hoc mixture-of-experts VLA for driving, which consolidates N independently finetuned per-domain models into a single multi-domain model from their weights and a small proxy set alone. When different operators finetune the same base model, their weight updates end up sharing a lot of structure. We exploit this by decomposing all the updates together using singular value decomposition (SVD), splitting each one into a shared part (the same across all domains) and a tiny domain-specific part. The router then only needs to work with those tiny domain-specific pieces, not the full expert weights, which is what keeps the approach efficient. Then two cooperating clip-level blind routers, one over the VLM reasoning experts and one over the flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset. Across six diverse domains spanning urban, off-road, and highway driving on cars, trucks, and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of the per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized, and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost. Adding a new domain requires only projecting its weight update onto the shared basis with no end-to-end retraining needed. The resulting model also generalizes to domain combinations it was never explicitly trained on.

papers.title: Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation
papers.authors: Bingzhang Wang, Nathan Zhao, Jialeng Ni, Jiajin Zheng, Yin Zhang, Kehua Chen, Jian Yao
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.

papers.title: Data-Driven Precision Control of Soft Helicoid Robots
papers.authors: Roshan S. Kaundinya, Mark Leone, Roberto Sabella, Hugo Buurmeijer, Luis Pabon, John Irvin Alora, Marco Pavone, George Haller
papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.

papers.title: Dancing with REEM-C: A Robot-To-Human Physical-Social Communication Study
papers.authors: Marie Charbonneau, Francisco Javier Andrade Chavez, Katja Mombaur
papers.abstract: Humans often work closely together and relay a wealth of information through physical interaction. Robots, on the other hand, are not yet able to work similarly closely with humans and to effectively convey information when engaging in physical-social human-robot interaction (psHRI). This currently limits the potential of human-robot collaboration to solve real-world problems. This paper investigates how to establish clear and intuitive robot-to-human communication, while considering human comfort during psHRI. We approach this question from the perspective of a leader-follower dancing scenario, in which a full-body humanoid robot leads a human by signaling the next steps through a choice of communication modalities including haptic, visual, and audio signals. This is achieved through the development of a split whole-body control framework combining admittance and impedance control on the upper body, with position control on the lower body for balancing and stepping. Robot-led psHRI participant experiments allowed us to verify controller performance, as well as to build an understanding of what types of communication work better from the perspective of human partners, particularly in terms of perceived effectiveness and comfort.

papers.title: Curie's Jarvis: Autonomous Robotic Chemistry Experiments from Printed Protocols
papers.authors: Rumi Loghmani, Bozhang Song, Victor Alvarado, Aliyah Redding, Amir Barati Farimani
papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.

papers.title: Cultivating Resilience: Urban Agriculture and Vertical Farming for Food, Health, and Environment – A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Nur Aziizah Darwis, Sigit Bayu Cahyanto, Anggistina Wulansari, Syukur Rahmat Gulo, Ahmad Tohirin, Gunawan Gunawan, Taofik Krisdiyanto, Maria Virgine Lilyana Manumanas
papers.abstract: Background Urbanization and climate change pressure urban food systems. Urban agriculture and vertical farming integrate biological systems, smart technologies, architectural design, food engineering, and environmental management to enhance food security, public health, and environmental sustainability. However, the literature remains fragmented, and no synthesis has examined how these domains interact within a food, health, and environment nexus. Methods This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020. Scopus was searched using a four-block string covering urban agriculture, smart technologies, architecture and biology, and food, health, and environment. From 1,207 documents, after filtering (2016–2026, research articles, English, open access) and screening, 38 studies were included. Data extraction used a standardized form. Quality was assessed with MMAT, JBI, CASP, and ISO 14040/14044. Thematic synthesis addressed eight research questions. Results The 38 studies spanned Architecture (n = 14), IT/Computational Science (n = 8), PSDAL (n = 14), Breeding (n = 7), Biology (n = 7), Public Health (n = 5), and Food Science (n = 4). Quality assessment: 27 low risk, 11 moderate, none high. Key findings: 156% food self-sufficiency; 13.5–20.2% energy savings; 57.14% water savings; 14.1% CO2 reduction; 28.1% VOC reduction; 20.9% PM2.5 reduction; 7.8°C PET reduction; GWP 0.86 kg CO2-eq/MJ; NER 3.7. CRISPR crops, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, and microalgae improved crop architecture, nutrient uptake, and resource recovery. IoT, AI, digital twins, and robotics enabled precision monitoring and control. Green façades, BIPV, agrivoltaics, and green roofs created multifunctional envelopes. Conclusions Urban agriculture and vertical farming yield synergistic benefits across food, health, and environment. Evidence supports integration into sustainable urban development. Gaps remain: multi-climate validation, economic analysis, policy fragmentation, data standardisation, and social acceptance. Future research should prioritise multi-site validation, economic assessment, regulatory frameworks, data interoperability, and AI-driven optimisation. Cultivating resilience requires integrated, evidence-based approaches aligning biological potential, technological capability, and architectural design.

papers.title: Correctness Boundaries of Typed Plans for Natural-Language Robot Fleet Control
papers.authors: Artem Tuzov, Dmitrii Vizitei, Evgenii Shlomov, Senya Belykh, Anastasia Malakhova, Alexander Maloletov
papers.abstract: We examine what plan validation and execution reports establish in natural-language robot fleet control. Commands are traced through typed plans, deterministic corrections, fleet coordination and outcome checks in a three-level Robot Operating System 2 implementation with twenty simulated robots. An offline benchmark of 44 cases checks plan structure and selected command requirements. Across five local configurations without a response schema, 70.0-87.3% of responses pass. All runs in a selected 18-run simulation series meet their pose-based task conditions. This series includes two successful repeats that replaced incomplete runs after a software change. Saved plans and logs document duplicate pickup assignments and goal adjustments within the original task zones. Separate formation traces show a structurally accepted plan with the wrong formation shape and a rejected route, and an arrival report that omitted a requested robot after replanning. Carry completion records pickup and subsequent drop-off zone presence for the same robot. The cases distinguish changes to executable actions from changes to the requirements covered by a completion report. They motivate checking the effective assignments, goals and reported outcome against the original command.

papers.title: Compass 1: Towards Open-World and Persistent Embodied Navigation from Monocular RGB Videos
papers.authors: Hai Zhang, Siqi Liang, Yanjun Guo, Shoufeng Zhang, Yunhao Wang, Hangyu Du, Haoguang Mai, Hongchen Li, et al.
papers.abstract: Embodied navigation requires agents to achieve persistent spatial awareness and long-horizon execution stability in open-world environments. However, existing navigation architectures struggle to sustain both capabilities, remaining effective only over a handful of recent frames. We present Compass 1, the first embodied navigation foundation model to unify language understanding and video generation while enabling memory backtracking through nearly 2mins of visual history. Without altering the underlying architecture, we introduce History Representation, which integrates sparse visual keyframes with an explicit History Representation Map to preserve long-term spatiotemporal context. To effectively leverage this history, we further introduce History Utilization, a structured VQA supervision protocol comprising three categories: task-stage grounding, exploration consistency, and spatiotemporal target retrieval, enabling map-grounded reasoning and stable persistent long-horizon navigation. To fuel this system, we establish a complete annotation pipeline for monocular RGB videos and open-source a massive dataset featuring over 500 hours of high-quality real-world interactions and over 2,000 hours of annotated web videos. Trained mainly on the distribution of 1m height camera, Compass 1 generalizes seamlessly across diverse embodiments and scenarios, ranging from indoor environments to pedestrian-dense streets, spanning wheeled robot at 0.35m, quadruped dog at 0.5m, humanoid at 0.85m, and aerial drone at 1.5m. Compass 1achieves a dominant overall success rate of 79.4% across open-world evaluations, compared to 17.8% for the strongest baseline. It demonstrates exceptional zero-shot execution exceeding 90% on foundational tasks, a 250% boost in exploration, and an unparalleled leap from 0% to 58% in challenging persistent history backtracking.

papers.title: Compact and Wide-Force-Range Magnetorheological Hand Exoskeleton for Kinesthetic Feedback in Teleoperation
papers.authors: Xianlong Mai, Rui Yu, Rui Chen, Daniele Leonardis, Wenbo Li, Domenico Chiaradia, Antonio Frisoli, Shuaishuai Sun
papers.abstract: Hand kinesthetic feedback is crucial for restoring and enhancing human perception of force and displacement in robotic hand teleoperation. Wide perception range of force feedback is vital in rendering objects of different stiffness, especially for high-stiffness rendering. However, existing approaches struggle to achieve wide range of force feedback while maintaining compact and wearable design. This paper presents a hand exoskeleton system employing magnetorheological (MR) brakes to provide a wide range kinesthetic feedback during teleoperation. The MR brake provides a braking torque ranging from 0.01 to 0.918 Nm, while maintaining a compact structure with a total mass of only 39.8 g. The proposed exoskeleton can render fingertip forces up to 21 N while maintaining back-driving force of 1.01 N. Experimental results show that the system allows users to discriminate object stiffness using kinesthetic feedback alone. In a tele-grasping task, when both conditions achieved a 100% success rate, kinesthetic feedback led to a 28.2% reduction in object contact force compared to visual feedback only, enhancing object safety and operator immersion. Questionnaire results further indicate that kinesthetic feedback improves reliability, realism, and user confidence during teleoperation.

papers.title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics
papers.authors: Sepideh Ravanbakhsh, Hamidreza Moradi
papers.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

papers.title: CSG-Nav: Confidence-Aware Semantic-Geometric Fusion for Robust Exploration and Accurate Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation
papers.authors: Shoubin Chen, Rui Xu, Zehao Wu, Kai Zhang, Tao Huang, Zhou Liu, Qingquan Li
papers.abstract: Zero-shot object-goal navigation requires autonomous agents to explore unseen environments and locate target objects without task-specific training, posing challenges in perceptual reliability under observation uncertainty and physically grounded goal termination. Although foundation-model-based approaches improve generalization, they remain vulnerable to unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-induced directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect stopping decisions. To address these limitations, we propose CSG-Nav, a zero-shot navigation framework centered on confidence-aware multimodal information fusion. CSG-Nav integrates three complementary fusion mechanisms. First, semantic-source fusion integrates open-vocabulary detection results, detection confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning to produce more reliable direction-level semantic scores and suppress hallucination-induced directional bias. Second, spatial-confidence fusion weights multi-view semantic evidence using a Gaussian decay function, suppressing unreliable distant observations while accumulating spatially consistent exploration preferences. Third, semantic-geometric decision fusion combines semantic target detection with depth-based 3D localization to support physically grounded stopping decisions. Experiments on HM3Dv1, HM3Dv2, and MP3D demonstrate competitive zero-shot performance, achieving success rates of 58.9%, 71.6%, and 44.3%. Fusion-level ablations and real-world deployments in indoor and outdoor environments further verify the effectiveness and practicality of CSG-Nav for robust navigation under uncertain perception. Code is available at https://xr-ui.github.io/CSGNav.github.io/

papers.title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation
papers.authors: Reece Keller, Declan Kutscher, Xaq Pitkow, Aran Nayebi
papers.abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

papers.title: Budget-aware Correspondence-driven View Selection for Real-time 3D Perception of Mobile Robots
papers.authors: Vaishnav Ramesh, Jacob Carter, Shivali J. Patel, Sanjeev J. Koppal, Md Jahidul Islam
papers.abstract: 3D visual perception and scene reconstruction are critical for autonomous robots and intelligent transportation, yet real-world deployments often generate long, redundant image sequences that hinder downstream processing. This report investigates BCVS (budget-aware correspondence-driven view sampling), a pose-free view selection algorithm that offers 22+ FPS on a CPU, enabling online filtering for efficient 3D perception by mobile robots. Unlike existing approaches that rely on full structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines or camera pose estimation, BCVS employs a purely correspondence-based scoring strategy that prioritizes view novelty while maintaining sufficient overlap for geometric stability. Given a user-specified budget, BCVS iteratively selects the most distinct frames and suppresses near-duplicates, producing compact subsets that preserve connectivity and minimize reconstruction loss. Extensive experiments on benchmark show that BCVS outperforms CPU-friendly baselines at tight budgets and remains competitive as budgets scale. Field trials with large aerial and marine robotics data further validate its practicality and scalability: BCVS reduces redundancy up to 16% while sustaining robust SfM registration and high-quality 3D reconstructions.

papers.title: Bridging Task Planning and Execution for Language-Conditioned Bimanual Manipulation
papers.authors: Emanuele Cuzzocrea, Giuseppina Iannotti, Luca Rossini, Arturo Laurenzi, Nikos Tsagarakis
papers.abstract: Robots are increasingly expected to execute natural-language manipulation tasks in real-world environments. This is particularly relevant in household assistance and logistics, where clutter requires reasoning about both task objectives and execution feasibility. This challenge becomes even more pronounced for bimanual humanoid platforms, where coordinating two manipulators introduces additional interaction and kinematic constraints. We present a zero-shot vision-language framework for execution-aware bimanual manipulation that jointly reasons about task objectives and physical feasibility. Planning is grounded in a structured scene representation that combines semantic object relations with execution constraints, enabling the selection of obstacle relocations and execution choices while preserving task semantics. Compatible actions are organised into parallel bimanual stages with explicit pre- and post-conditions. A hierarchical validator evaluates these conditions under perceptual uncertainty and uses stage-level execution history to support local recovery or targeted replanning. Experiments on the CENTAURO hybrid wheeled-legged humanoid robot across nine language-conditioned manipulation scenarios show higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline. In dedicated failure scenarios, hierarchical validation recovers from execution failures with fewer model queries than always replanning. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining execution reasoning directly into task planning. papers.title: BioMARS 2.0: a robotic biologist for formulating and adapting biological experiments
papers.authors: Yibo Qiu, Zan Huang, Yilin Qiao, Ziyang Ling, Yi Wang, Zhengyang Lu, Hangke Peng, Haoliang Ye, et al.
