papers.title: Moving Heads, Moving Sounds: Systematic Errors in Auditory Motion Perception
papers.authors: Timo Oess, Laurence R. Harris, Marc O. Ernst
papers.abstract: The movement of moving objects seen during self-motion is incorrectly perceived as a result of errors in parsing the visual motion arising from the retina and from information about the movement of the head and eyes in space1. The perception of motion of auditory targets may be even more challenging as previous research suggests that the auditory system lacks dedicated low-level speed processing mechanisms. This study investigates how the perception of a moving auditory sound source is influenced by concurrent head movements, drawing comparisons with established visual motion perception findings and illusions, such as the Filehne Illusion. Participants were asked to move their heads at a fixed speed, either horizontally (left to right or right to left) or vertically (up to down or down to up), while indicating the perceived direction of a moving sound source by using a joystick. A physical sound source was moved silently at a constant speed in fronto-parallel 2D space using a 3x3x3m cable robot. Results showed that head movements created a perceptual bias of the perceived direction of the moving sound source in the opposite direction to the head movement. Responses were less precise during horizontal than vertical head movement, whereas overall directional accuracy did not differ reliably between movement planes. The magnitude of the directional error also depended on the direction of head movement, consistent with the different cues available for horizontal and vertical localization (binaural vs. spectral cues). These findings suggest that similarly to how visual motion perception is distorted by extraretinal signals and the movement of the eyes, so too is auditory motion perception influenced by movement of the ears, revealing errors in the integration of proprioceptive, vestibular and auditory cues that distort the perceived direction of a moving sound source.

papers.title: Mobility Information Capacity of Multi-Robot Systems: Safety-Aware Maneuver Design
papers.authors: Weijie Yuan
papers.abstract: Multiple robots operating in shared workspaces must adjust their speed, direction, and trajectories to coordinate with one another and respond to changing tasks and disturbances. The available maneuver freedom depends on the dynamics, uncertainty, and safety margins, even for a fixed fleet size and workspace. However, robot count, workspace occupancy, and task throughput do not quantify how much the fleet can vary its motion or how reliably these variations can be observed. We develop a mobility information capacity (MIC) framework that jointly characterizes these two aspects. Mobility information is defined as the mutual information between a joint maneuver sequence and its noisy trajectory observation, and MIC maximizes this quantity under maneuver-resource constraints. For a linear Gaussian maneuver-to-observation model with feedback dynamics, we characterize the finite-horizon information benchmark and derive its stationary long-horizon spectral limit, accounting for heterogeneous mobility gains, colored uncertainty, and temporally coupled maneuver costs. We further map workspace-boundary, inter-robot separation, and actuator chance constraints into coupled maneuver-covariance restrictions and derive conditions under which covariance optimization reduces to resource allocation across mobility modes. Finite joint maneuver codebooks are then constructed through individual risk screening and noise-whitened trajectory separation, with bounds linking sequence recovery error and achieved information to the capacity benchmarks. An aerial-robot simulation study evaluates spectral convergence, safety-aware allocation, finite-codebook identification, and fleet-size scaling. The resulting framework complements occupancy and task-throughput measures by quantifying the maximum observable maneuver freedom supported by a mobility system.

papers.title: MetaNav: Metacognitive Vision-Language Navigation via Reflective Exploration
papers.authors: Xueying Li, Feng Lyu, Hao Wu, Mingliu Liu, Jia-Nan Liu, Guozi Liu
papers.abstract: Training-free Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) agents powered by foundation models can follow instructions and explore 3D environments. However, existing approaches rely on greedy frontier selection and passive spatial memory, leading to inefficient behaviors such as local oscillation and redundant revisiting. We argue that this stems from a lack of metacognitive capabilities: the agent cannot monitor its exploration progress, diagnose strategy failures, or adapt accordingly. To address this, we propose MetaNav, a metacognitive navigation agent integrating spatial memory, history-aware planning, and reflective correction. Spatial memory builds a persistent 3D semantic map. History-aware planning penalizes revisiting to improve efficiency. Reflective correction detects stagnation and uses an LLM to generate corrective rules that guide future frontier selection. Experiments on GOAT-Bench, HM3D-OVON, and A-EQA show that MetaNav achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing VLM queries by 20.7%, demonstrating that metacognitive reasoning significantly improves robustness and efficiency.

papers.title: Maze Runner: Autonomous Maze Navigation with Line-Based Localization and Control Barrier Functions
papers.authors: Alvaro J. Gaona, Lucas Gómez-Velayos, Peter Pasuy-Quevedo
papers.abstract: Maze navigation requires localization from sparse, repetitive geometry, planning through narrow corridors, and control that stays safe when the estimate or the map is wrong. We present Maze Runner, an open autonomy stack in C++ and ROS 2 that addresses these needs end to end on a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL with a 2D LiDAR in Gazebo. Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online. Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*. A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) tracks the plan while discrete-time Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on world-frame LiDAR points keep the robot clear of walls and unmapped obstacles. The algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested core library, and the whole stack builds and runs from a single reproducible environment. In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget.

papers.title: MDF++: Visuo-Tactile World Action Model with End-to-end Representation Learning
papers.authors: Zixuan Huang, Jinhao Yu, Zachary Charlick, Dmitry Berenson
papers.abstract: Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physicallygrounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. We evaluate MDF++ on a suite of contact-rich manipulation tasks, including realworld bolt screwing and nut mating, and show that it outperforms WAMs built on frozen pretrained representations by up to 50%. papers.title: Look Before Acting: Enhancing Vision Foundation Representations for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Yulin Luo, Hao Chen, Zhuangzhe Wu, Bowen Sui, Jiaming Liu Jiaming Liu, Chenyang Gu, Zhuoyang Liu, Peng Jia
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, in which reliable action prediction critically depends on accurately interpreting and integrating visual observations conditioned on language instructions. Although recent works have sought to enhance the visual capabilities of VLA models, most approaches treat the LLM backbone as a black box, providing limited insight into how visual information is grounded into action generation. Therefore, we perform a systematic analysis of multiple VLA models across different action-generation paradigms and observe that sensitivity to visual tokens progressively decreases in deeper layers during action generation. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{DeepVision-VLA}, built on a \textbf{Vision-Language Mixture-of-Transformers (VL-MoT)} framework. This framework enables shared attention between the vision foundation model and the VLA backbone, injecting multi-level visual features from the vision expert into deeper layers of the VLA backbone to enhance visual representations for precise and complex manipulation. In addition, we introduce \textbf{Action-Guided Visual Pruning (AGVP)}, which leverages shallow-layer attention to prune irrelevant visual tokens while preserving task-relevant ones, reinforcing critical visual cues for manipulation with minimal computational overhead. DeepVision-VLA outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods by 9.0\% and 7.5\% on simulated and real-world tasks, respectively, providing new insights for the design of visually enhanced VLA models.

papers.title: Lodos: A Lightweight Simulator Designed for Contact-Rich Interactions with Detailed Meshes
papers.authors: Onur Beker, Andreas René Geist, Georg Martius
papers.abstract: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.

papers.title: Locating Contact on Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots From Tendon Measurements Alone via Constrained Moving Horizon Estimation
papers.authors: Haitham El-Hussieny
papers.abstract: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Without contact, the MHE offered no advantage over the EKF, which confirms that its benefit comes from the contact constraints. This report extends a letter submitted to IEEE Control Systems Letters with complete proofs and additional experiments.

papers.title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, Faisal Aqlan
papers.abstract: Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under "not X" and "X". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.

papers.title: Lightweight Path-Aware Frontier Re-ranking for LiDAR-Based UAV Exploration
papers.authors: Duc Manh Do, Thanh Nguyen Canh, Ngoc Minh Do, Mai Thanh Thai, Xiem HoangVan
papers.abstract: Autonomous 3D exploration with UAVs requires efficient target selection under limited flight time and onboard computation. In conventional Euclidean-distance-based frontier pipelines, geometric distance may poorly represent the actual collision-free travel cost in cluttered environments, leading to inefficient frontier choices. This paper presents a lightweight path-aware frontier re-ranking method for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. The method first retains a small top-N set of promising frontier candidates using a lightweight utility function and then applies time-bounded RRT* planning to estimate their feasible path costs for re-ranking. The path generated for the selected frontier is further reused for navigation to reduce redundant global planning. Experiments in three warehouse-like environments show that the proposed method consistently produces shorter exploration trajectories than conventional frontier baselines, with traveled-distance reductions of up to 14.1%, while reducing exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments and remaining competitive in the third. The method maintains map detail comparable to the conventional OctoMap-based baseline, demonstrating an effective trade-off between exploration efficiency and mapping quality.

papers.title: Latent-WAM: Latent World Action Modeling for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Linbo Wang, Yupeng Zheng, Qiang Chen, Shiwei Li, Yichen Zhang, Zebin Xing, Qichao Zhang, Xiang Li
papers.abstract: We introduce Latent-WAM, an efficient end-to-end autonomous driving framework that achieves strong trajectory planning through spatially-aware and dynamics-informed latent world representations. Existing world-model-based planners suffer from inadequately compressed representations, limited spatial understanding, and underutilized temporal dynamics, resulting in sub-optimal planning under constrained data and compute budgets. Latent-WAM addresses these limitations with two core modules: a Spatial-Aware Compressive World Encoder (SCWE) that distills geometric knowledge from a foundation model and compresses multi-view images into compact scene tokens via learnable queries, and a Dynamic Latent World Model (DLWM) that employs a causal Transformer to autoregressively predict future world status conditioned on historical visual and ego status representations. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v2 and HUGSIM demonstrate new state-of-the-art results: 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 28.9 HD-Score on HUGSIM, surpassing the best prior perception-free method by 3.2 EPDMS with significantly less training data and a compact 104M-parameter model. The code and model weights have been open-sourced at https://github.com/yukki555/Latent-WAM.

papers.title: LACART: Lookahead-Augmented Collision Avoidance and Reference Tracking Strategies for Safety-Critical Robots
papers.authors: Pedro Lopes, Amit Shivam, Luis Tiago Paiva
papers.abstract: Autonomous racing provides a demanding testbed for collision avoidance under tight geometric and computational constraints. Building on a recent conference contribution and a master's dissertation, LACART combines lookahead-based control barrier functions (CBFs), a relaxed control Lyapunov function (CLF), and quadratic programming (QP) to modify nominal vehicle commands for obstacle avoidance and reference tracking. The method handles circular obstacles and track boundaries in a common optimisation layer. Comparative simulation results against Huang \emph{et al.} \cite{r9} show similar full-track paths and lower median computation times: 0.31 versus 0.33 ms per step and 0.023 versus 0.025 ms per QP solve. The dissertation further demonstrates a 1:43-scale vehicle with camera-based estimation and wireless actuation at a reported 25 Hz control rate. We identify the conditions linking lookahead-point clearance to body clearance, illustrate hardware limitations, and propose a recorded demonstration of safety intervention and recovery. The contribution targets ground-robot collision avoidance and real-time safety monitoring.

papers.title: It Takes Two to Tangram: Multi-Agent Object Centric Reinforcement Learning for Assembly
papers.authors: Paul Knaußt, Kay Pompetzki, Nico Bohlinger, Niklas Funk, Cristiana de Farias, Rolf Findeisen, Jan Peters
papers.abstract: Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances. To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control. A graph neural network represents the pieces, their target poses, and their spatial relationships, and predicts translational and angular velocities for each component. Per-agent proximal policy optimization with a centralized graph critic directly learns motion and temporal coordination within a single feedback policy. We study this formulation through planar Tangram assembly, where pieces must slide and rotate into a given configuration while remaining on the assembly surface. Procedural generation of target configurations and randomized initial arrangements support training and evaluation across diverse assembly problems. Our experiments isolate the roles of relational structure and multi-agent optimization, and compare learned control with sampling-based planning. We demonstrate concurrent assembly in simulation and transfer the policy to sequential execution on a real robot, as our object-centric formulation decouples learned assembly coordination from low-level physical control. papers.title: InstantHMR : Real-Time Human Mesh Recovery on Your Phone
papers.authors: Mohamed Adjel, Kahina Chalabi, Vincent Bonnet
papers.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.

papers.title: Horizon-Coupled Obstacle Guidance for Relative-Action Diffusion Policies
papers.authors: Guangyuan Wang, Haishan Xia, Zitao Zhang, Kejia Chen, Yuanchen Sun, Zhenguo Sun, Donghao Zhang, Yu Zhang, et al.
papers.abstract: Real-world robot deployment requires adapting learned policies to unseen obstacles without collecting new demonstrations or retraining. Existing policy-level guidance often applies obstacle corrections independently at individual horizon steps, which may address local obstacle violations but fail to coordinate the action sequence into a complete, task-directed detour. How obstacle responses should be propagated across the action horizon to coordinate complete, task-directed avoidance motion remains underexplored. We introduce an inferencetime obstacle-guidance framework for pretrained relative-action diffusion policies. It rolls out cumulative relative actions into a workspace trajectory, evaluates obstacle interactions along the trajectory with an SDF-based obstacle model, and propagates each obstacle response to all contributing action increments during denoising. Real-robot experiments across seven obstacleconstrained scenarios spanning four manipulation tasks show that our method achieves 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free task successes, compared with 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action pointwise guidance. Ablations show that the relative-action horizoncoupled formulation provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.

papers.title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
papers.authors: Ramy ElMallah, Marc Bishara, Hyegang Kim, Yuxi Zhang, Chongyu Zhu, Chi-Guhn Lee
papers.abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.

papers.title: HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
papers.authors: Boran Zhao, Yanbin Hu, Jun Ye, Zhenxian Hu, Yuxin Zhai, Jin Cui, Pengju Ren
papers.abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

papers.title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
papers.authors: Hongkun Yu, Francisco M. López, Francisco Cruz
papers.abstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.

papers.title: Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Xun Tu, Minghao Zou, Karthik Desingh
papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: https://rpm-lab-umn.github.io/Grasp-TAGS-web-page/

papers.title: From virtual pets to AI companions: A relational-design framework for human–artificial bonds
papers.authors: Fernando Coura Assis
papers.abstract: Artificial companions occupy a hybrid position between interactive systems and social partners, yet research remains divided across virtual pets, social robots, relational agents, mixed-reality animals, and generative AI companions. This critical integrative review asks which design properties can make sustained human–artificial relationships possible without assuming that relational significance depends on human likeness or technical sophistication. It develops a five-dimensional relational-design framework: temporal continuity; legible need and vulnerability; contingent responsiveness; social presence and anthropomorphic interpretation; and recurrent care and support. A central revision to the framework is that care is not necessarily directed from the human toward the artificial entity. In many relational-agent, health, educational, and companionship contexts, the human is the recipient of support, and the system must detect, interpret, and respond to human needs. The framework therefore treats care as directional and potentially reciprocal, while distinguishing companion relationships from training simulations in which a virtual patient or student is primarily an object of professional practice. Drawing on research in virtual pets, social responses to computers, relational agents, human–robot interaction, digital possessions, and AI companions, the review connects each dimension to identifiable literature and illustrates its operation across different system types. It also examines well-being, asymmetrical power, vulnerable populations, loss, and platform governance. The framework is a conceptual tool rather than a validated measurement instrument; its value lies in generating comparative hypotheses and design questions that can be tested longitudinally and across contexts.

papers.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
papers.authors: Jingdong Zhang, Jionghao Wang, Zhengming Yu, Yancheng Cai, Wei Chow, Chris Choy, Zhiyang Dou, Hang Hua, et al.
papers.abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.

papers.title: FASTFUNNELS: Agile Multi Robot Navigation in Narrow Spaces via Adaptive Dynamic Funnels
papers.authors: Vignesh Rajagopal, Rohan Chandra
papers.abstract: We focus on the problem of high-speed multi-robot navigation in cluttered spaces with tight spatial constraints. A key challenge is balancing safety with agility, as existing methods often trade one for the other (slowing down near a bottleneck to avoid collisions versus failing to swerve in time at high speeds), especially for car-like systems. Our approach belongs to the family of formation control methods, in which Ackermann-steering agents coordinate while navigating tight spaces. However, current formation control techniques rely on rigid, pre-defined shapes and transitions that depend on initial conditions, the environment, and vehicle dynamics, and are impractical to maintain at high speeds. For example, agents passing through a small gap must first form a square, transform into a line using analytical equations, and then return to a square. In contrast, our approach is inspired by a droplet of water that continuously adapts its shape to the space it flows through without slowing down. We propose a hierarchical algorithm in which, at the high level, a reinforcement learning policy produces a dynamic, blob-like elliptical patch that morphs its shape in real time, squeezing, stretching, and orienting itself around obstacles and through tight spaces. At the low level, the robots are controlled via distributed model predictive control (DMPC) to stay inside the patch, which acts as a soft forcing function, while avoiding collisions with each other. We evaluate our approach, FastFunnels, on simulated F1TENTH racing cars across 14 scenarios with N=1 to N=6 robots, averaged over 20 trials each. FastFunnels achieves an 89% completion rate at 7.73 m/s, while all baselines either fail to complete the track or succeed only at very low speeds (0.07-1.79 m/s, about 40% completion rate).

papers.title: Exo2EgoPose: Leveraging Exocentric Demonstrations for Vision-Language guided Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Forecasting
papers.authors: Zhaofeng Shi, Heqian Qiu, Lanxiao Wang, Xiang Li, Hongliang Li
papers.abstract: Perceiving multimodal cues and forecasting fine-grained actions from an egocentric (Ego) perspective is vital for applications like robot manipulation. However, previous studies either rely mainly on under-informed visual inputs to predict coarse human motions or follow the VRM/VLA paradigm, which suffers from insufficient robot data and the gap between human and robot embodiments. We observe that 3D hand pose naturally serves as a unified representation to bridge human-robot actions. Hence, we investigate an under-explored Vision-Language guided Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Forecasting (VL-EHPF) task, which aims to predict future Ego 3D hand poses from visual observations, a language instruction, and pose states. To overcome the limited field-of-view and highly dynamic motions in the Ego view, we propose a framework dubbed Exo2EgoPose, which innovatively leverages holistic and stable exocentric (Exo) demonstrations as guidance to compensate for partial and dynamic Ego-view cues. Specifically, we introduce a Dual-level Exocentric Reconstruction Module (DERM), which incorporates the paired Exo videos as supervision to reconstruct their video-level and chunked frame-level representations, thereby modeling spatial contexts and temporal dynamics. Then, the Global-to-Local Modulation Module (GLMM) utilizes the reconstructed hierarchical Exo representations for progressive feature refinement via attention mechanisms and adaptive modulation, enabling comprehensive Exo guidance for accurate Ego hand pose forecasting. Extensive experiments on \textit{AssemblyHands}, \textit{Ego-Exo4D}, and our newly constructed \textit{EgoMe-pose} benchmarks show the superiority of our method, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin. Moreover, it demonstrates an effective human-to-robot transfer capability and yields improvements on the \textit{CALVIN} dataset.

papers.title: Evaluating augmented reality evacuation guidance system for sustaining compliance under social interference in virtual environment
papers.authors: Junyoung Kim, Jeongjun Park, MoonSeo Park, Changbum R. Ahn, Ilhwa Lee
papers.abstract: Evacuation guidance systems provide routes during emergencies, but occupants do not always comply when social cues compete with guidance. Limited research has examined attention allocation and sustained compliance across multiple decision points. This study compared environment-embedded cues (CON), AR navigation (AR-NAV), and a socially embodied AR virtual safety manager (AR-VSM) in an immersive VR evacuation experiment under competing environmental and social cues. Both AR conditions were simulated through a virtual smartphone interface. These conditions showed lower attention to surrounding non-player characters (NPCs), while AR-VSM yielded the highest sustained compliance. NPC-oriented attention was strongly negatively associated with compliance. An exploratory mediation analysis suggested statistical associations among guidance condition, attention, and compliance without establishing a causal mechanism. These findings highlight the relevance of attention allocation and guidance design to sustained compliance under competing local cues.

papers.title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

papers.title: EmoBench-M: Benchmarking Emotional Intelligence for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.authors: He Hu, Lianzhong You, Hongbo Xu, Qianning Wang, Fei Richard Yu, Fei Ma, Zebang Cheng, Zheng Lian
papers.abstract: With the integration of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) into robotic systems and AI applications, embedding emotional intelligence (EI) capabilities is essential for enabling these models to perceive, interpret, and respond to human emotions effectively in real-world scenarios. Existing static, text-based, or text-image benchmarks overlook the multimodal complexities of real interactions and fail to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of emotional expressions, rendering them inadequate for evaluating MLLMs' EI capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce EmoBench-M, a systematic benchmark grounded in established psychological theories, designed to evaluate MLLMs across 13 evaluation scenarios spanning three hierarchical dimensions: foundational emotion recognition (FER), conversational emotion understanding (CEU), and socially complex emotion analysis (SCEA). Evaluation was conducted on 27 state-of-the-art MLLMs, using both objective task-specific metrics and LLM-based evaluation, revealing a substantial performance gap relative to human-level competence. Even the best performing models, Gemini-3.0-Pro and GPT-5.2, achieve the highest scores on EmoBench-M, 70.5 and 66.5 points respectively. Specialized models such as AffectGPT exhibit uneven performance across EmoBench-M, demonstrating strengths in certain scenarios but generally lacking comprehensive emotional intelligence. By providing a comprehensive, multimodal evaluation framework, EmoBench-M captures both the strengths and weaknesses of current MLLMs across diverse emotional contexts. All benchmark resources, including datasets and code, are publicly available at https://emo-gml.github.io/, facilitating further research and advancement in MLLM emotional intelligence.

papers.title: Emo-LiveSync: Real-Time Universal Lip Synchronization with Explicit Emotion Control
papers.authors: Sangjoon Yu, Seungeun Lee, JoonHeyok Shin, Ji-Su Kang
papers.abstract: Lip synchronization, the task of generating realistic lip movements synchronized with audio signals, is fundamental to applications such as film dubbing, virtual avatars, and digital content creation. Recent GAN-based methods offer computational efficiency but often lack visual fidelity, while diffusion-based approaches achieve high-quality results at the cost of substantial computational overhead. Moreover, most existing methods are limited to photo-realistic human faces, restricting their applicability to stylized characters and non-human entities. In this paper, we propose an efficient universal lip-sync video generation framework that achieves high-quality results without compromising computational efficiency. We build on LivePortrait, a warp-based portrait animation model, and introduce a training strategy that aligns audio signals to an implicit motion space by distilling knowledge from a pre-trained video-to-motion model. This enables real-time inference while maintaining high visual fidelity, and naturally generalizes to diverse stylistic characters beyond photo-realistic humans. Furthermore, we introduce an expressive control gate that enables explicit manipulation of emotional expressions for content enrichment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both visual quality and lip-sync accuracy while ensuring real-time inference.

papers.title: Editorial: Bridging barriers: technology integration in mathematics education
papers.authors: Musa Adekunle Ayanwale, Gladys Sunzuma, Brantina Chirinda
papers.abstract: Digital technologies can expand the ways learners encounter, represent and investigate mathematics. Their educational value, however, depends on the conditions under which these possibilities become meaningful learning opportunities. Connectivity, teacher preparation, curriculum demands and the authority assigned to technological outputs all shape what learners can do with digital resources. The central challenge is therefore to connect technological possibilities with mathematically purposeful, equitable and sustainable teaching. This Research Topic brings together 21 contributions examining that challenge across school, university and teacher education settings. Its scope encompasses dynamic geometry, simulations, digital video, blended learning, intelligent tutoring, generative artificial intelligence (AI) and computational approaches to educational evaluation. Across these varied contributions, a common proposition emerges meaningful integration requires attention to mathematical reasoning, teacher agency, contextual conditions and the quality of evidence used to guide decisions.Several contributions examine how digital representations support access to mathematical ideas. In Uganda, Kirabo et al. report higher post-test performance among in-service primary teachers participating in GeoGebra-supported problem-based learning than among comparison participants. Observations suggest that visualisation, collaboration and application contributed to the learning environment. Similarly, Zenteno Ruiz et al. report favourable achievement outcomes following a PhET-supported intervention on mathematical functions among Peruvian university students. These studies support further investigation of approaches that coordinate interactive representations with structured mathematical tasks, while leaving the respective contributions of software and pedagogy to be established more precisely.Visualisation also offers routes into abstract logical and spatial relationships. Orhani et al. document improved performance and positive attitudes following instruction on De Morgan's Laws using visual methods. Their single-group design, however, cannot isolate the intervention from other explanations for change. In synchronous online geometry instruction, Yeung et al. connect GeoGebra applets, varied examples and classroom interaction with gains in achievement and cognitive engagement among 19 students, with achievement maintained at a two-week delayed assessment. The small exploratory setting warrants caution in extending these results to routine provision.Other contributions broaden the account of what representation involves. Villa-Ochoa and Farsani analyse prospective teachers' mathematical modelling videos, showing how audiovisual production can organise meanings about mathematics and its relevance to lived experience. Videla et al. examine material construction, AI-mediated bodily classification and immersive virtual reality through an ecological and embodied perspective. Their analysis locates geometric understanding within coordinated action involving learners, tasks and environments. Together, these contributions invite teachers to design opportunities for learners to manipulate, explain and construct mathematical relationships, with explicit attention to how representations support reasoning.The availability of sophisticated resources does not ensure that teachers can use them effectively. Professional learning must also provide opportunities to exercise that competence. Mensah shows how a tightly controlled GeoGebra model lesson can demonstrate procedures while restricting prospective teachers' participation in the reasoning behind instructional decisions. This analysis highlights a barrier within teacher education itself: observation of competent performance may offer limited opportunities to develop autonomous pedagogical judgement.Complementary approaches emphasise creation and reflection. Huang et al. analyse GeoGebra artefacts and micro-teaching videos from a year-long professional development programme, using visual learning analytics to inform recommendations for open educational resources and practices. In Zimbabwe, Jamba and Chauraya describe how collaborative STEAM activities involving digital and AI tools supported prospective teachers' reported conceptual reconstruction, explanatory flexibility and critical digital literacy. Across these studies, a productive direction for professional learning is sustained participation in designing, testing, discussing and revising mathematically purposeful lessons.Equity requires attention to the material conditions of participation. In rural South African schools, Mulovhedzi identifies interacting infrastructure, pedagogical and leadership constraints, alongside adaptive practices such as offline preparation and device-sharing. Such responses demonstrate local expertise, but their necessity should also inform investment in dependable infrastructure and continuing instructional support.Participation presents additional challenges even where technologies are available. Yanisko et al. examine students' experiences of an engineering-embedded algebra elective in urban high schools. Students valued digital tools, practical tasks and real-world relevance, while also reporting difficulty and resistance to interdisciplinary demands. Their accounts suggest that access to demanding mathematical activity must be accompanied by scaffolding, clear expectations and responsive teaching.At university level, Kämpf et al. describe a spiral-curricular blended learning course linking mathematical methods with physics. Positive course evaluations and evidence of knowledge consolidation illustrate the potential of coordinated sequencing and interactive materials. Collectively, these contributions suggest that sustainable provision depends on curriculum coherence, usable resources and support for learners' participation over time. Open resources can contribute to this agenda when teachers have the capacity and time to adapt them to their learners and settings.The collection distinguishes promising applications of AI from the evidence needed to justify their use. In the related STEM domain of computer-robotics programming, Omeh and Ayanwale report favourable engagement, motivation and achievement outcomes for AI-supported problem-based learning. Because instructional conditions were located in different universities, institutional differences remain an alternative explanation. The findings motivate further controlled investigation of AI-supported scaffolding and collaboration, including their applicability to mathematics education.Generative AI also creates a need for critical evaluation of mathematical outputs. Mahlaba finds variation in how prospective teachers evaluated ChatGPT-generated word-problem solutions. Some identified and corrected errors, whereas others accepted inaccurate reasoning or relied on superficial judgements. Individually constructed prompts produced different outputs, limiting direct comparison across participants. The study nevertheless draws attention to the importance of mathematical knowledge and metacognitive monitoring in evaluating AI responses.Assessment applications require equally careful scrutiny. Ableitinger and Dorner identify handwriting-recognition errors, symbol misinterpretations and inconsistent error classifications when using GPT-4 Turbo to code students' solutions. These findings concern a particular model and workflow, yet they establish an enduring evaluation requirement: automated classifications must be checked against defensible human judgements for the intended tasks and learners. Teachers and researchers should retain responsibility for interpreting errors and deciding how feedback or scores will be used.Two contributions challenge the assumption that increased technology use necessarily produces greater learning. Using Japanese PISA data, Zhang et al. report that mathematics self-efficacy was a stronger predictor of achievement than the included ICT variables, with associations differing across types of ICT use. These observational results do not establish causal effects or mediation. In a longitudinal study of 940 students across 55 German classes, Schaaf et al. find no statistically significant association between intelligent tutoring system usage frequency and learning gains at the individual or class level. This result directs attention towards task selection, feedback uptake and instructional integration, while avoiding a general conclusion that tutoring systems are ineffective.Sound implementation decisions also depend on sound measurement. Susanibar Ramirez et al. adapted a questionnaire assessing teachers' reported AI use in Peru. The study contributes a contextually adapted instrument and evidence of internal consistency, although reported confirmatory fit indices indicate substantial model misfit. Further structural evaluation and independent validation are needed before using its scores for consequential comparisons or decisions. Reliability alone cannot establish the adequacy of the proposed score interpretations.Bian and Fang extend the methodological discussion through double/debiased machine learning for textbook evaluation. Flexible estimation can reduce dependence on restrictive functional forms, but causal interpretation still requires defensible identification assumptions. Across the collection, methodological advances are most valuable when the research design, measurement and analytical assumptions support the educational claim being made.Across these contributions, the educational promise of technology emerges through the interaction of mathematical tasks, teacher judgement, learner participation and institutional conditions. Dynamic representations, multimodal production and AI-supported activities offer opportunities to investigate and communicate mathematical ideas. Their benefits remain contingent on pedagogical design, reliable access and critical evaluation. The collection also identifies limits to the available evidence: favourable perceptions do not establish learning gains, usage frequency does not establish instructional quality, and internal consistency does not establish valid score interpretations.Bridging barriers therefore requires coordinated attention to material provision, professional agency and the quality of educational evidence. The central question for the field is under what conditions digital technologies expand equitable access to meaningful mathematical learning. Addressing this question calls for context-sensitive innovation accompanied by rigorous evaluation of sustained learning, accessibility and consequences.Educators and teacher educators should make mathematical reasoning the organising principle of technology-supported instruction. Professional development should provide sustained opportunities to co-design tasks, test representations, evaluate AI-generated solutions and revise lessons through classroom evidence and collaborative reflection.School leaders and policymakers should connect infrastructure investment with maintenance, technical support, protected professional learning time and curriculum alignment. Provision should include accessible resources and options suited to limited connectivity, with learners and teachers involved in identifying local priorities. Implementation should be judged by participation and learning opportunities, alongside availability and uptake.Researchers should strengthen comparative and longitudinal designs, account for classroom and institutional dependence, assess retention and transfer, and report implementation conditions transparently. Studies should investigate who benefits, who encounters barriers and which instructional processes explain differences. Instruments require independent validation and evidence supporting their intended interpretations and uses.Developers and institutions implementing AI should document system versions and relevant prompts, evaluate errors in the intended educational setting, protect learner data and maintain human responsibility for consequential decisions. We invite partnerships among teachers, learners, researchers, policymakers and developers to turn these priorities into locally responsive, sustainable practice. The shared goal is to make digital innovation accountable to mathematical understanding and equitable participation.

papers.title: EGT: Execution-Grounded Traversability through Learned Closed-Loop Trajectory Distributions
papers.authors: Chinmay Mundane, Amith Manoharan, Arun Kumar Singh
papers.abstract: Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle's motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements. We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%-39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%. Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24-42 and 30-44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.

papers.title: EA-Nav: Learning Safe Visual Navigation Policies with Embodiment Awareness
papers.authors: Jialu Zhang, Yong Du, Xianda Guo, Jituo Li, Shunwang Sun, Xinqi Liu, Yue Sun, Wei Sui
papers.abstract: Cross-embodiment navigation is a key challenge in embodied intelligence. Due to differences in embodiment, the same visual observation may imply different actions for different agents, making prediction ambiguous when relying solely on vision. Existing studies mainly rely on reinforcement learning, which requires large-scale interaction and careful reward design, making it difficult to support scalable pretraining and real-world adaptation. In contrast, imitation-learning-based approaches remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose an imitation-learning-based embodiment-aware navigation framework with a modular multi-stage design. In pretraining, we construct a cross-embodiment navigation dataset from Internet videos and introduce embodiment geometry as conditional tokens to reduce action ambiguity under the same observation. In fine-tuning, we design a multimodal information injection mechanism based on a decoupled architecture. Specifically, we design a trajectory augmentation strategy to generate high-risk samples, which are used to train spatial perception and risk-aware correction separately, thereby explicitly incorporating embodiment geometry for safe navigation. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively improves navigation performance across different embodiment settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating embodiment geometry into embodied navigation.

papers.title: DualTrust: Asymmetric Bayesian Reputation and Cryptographic Gating for Autonomous AI Agents
papers.authors: Khairan Noor Fadhlillah
papers.abstract: Abstract The proliferation of Ambient Wearable Intelligence (AWI) ecosystems, spanning augmented reality glasses, smartwatches, and pervasive edge IoT actuators, is fundamentally transitioning human-AI interaction from explicit tactile commands to continuous, implicit background tool delegation. In these ambient environments, autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are granted operational authority to invoke external APIs, reserve financial micro-quotas, and control physical actuators. However, existing safety guardrails depend on secondary LLM-as-a-judge classifiers that introduce prohibitive runtime latencies (400–850 ms) and recurring token expenses, while static role-based access control fails against continuous behavioral drift, memory backdoors, and interleaved salami-slicing exploits. We present DualTrust, an asymmetric Bayesian reputation and cryptographic gating runtime engineered for autonomous multi-agent containment. DualTrust enforces a decoupled principal-agent architecture that strictly isolates Human Principal Accountable Credit from Bayesian Agent Operational Standing. Agent behavior is continuously modulated via an asymmetric power-law slashing engine (Δβ ∝ (sev · c^2) · v_a^1.8) with instantaneous clean-streak reset, deterministic SHA-256 64-bucket striped concurrency locks, atomically locked rollback refunds, and an O(1) RAM sliding-window RFC 6962 Merkle audit ledger with rolling epoch seals that bounds active memory consumption by committing historical roots to persistent storage. Evaluated across 176 automated invariant tests and 10,000-cycle Monte Carlo attack simulations, DualTrust makes deterministic authorization verdicts in a median latency of 47.10 µs in-memory (mean 63.16 µs, tail p99 287.10 µs) and 155.80 µs under persistent SQLite WAL disk transactions, with end-to-end Python decorator wrappers executing in median 60.70 µs (async) and 88.30 µs (sync) without external API calls. Compared against state-of-the-art LLM guardrails, DualTrust achieves over 6,600× lower latency (and over 32× to 50× lower latency than localized AST validators), by policy construction blocks Sybil defamation against collusive probation swarms, and provides tamper-evident, append-only audit durability with RFC 6962 inclusion verification, establishing a practical, foundational governance runtime for trustworthy ambient intelligence.

papers.title: Driving with DINO: Vision Foundation Features as a Unified Bridge for Sim-to-Real Generation in Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Xuyang Chen, C.J. Zhang, Chuanheng Fu, Zihao Yang, Kaixuan Zhou, Yizhi Zhang, Yanfeng Zhang, Mingwei Sun
papers.abstract: Driven by the emergence of Controllable Video Diffusion, existing Sim2Real methods for autonomous driving video generation typically rely on explicit intermediate representations to bridge the domain gap. However, these modalities face a fundamental Consistency-Realism Dilemma. Low-level signals (e.g., edges, blurred images) ensure precise control but compromise realism by "baking in" synthetic artifacts, whereas high-level priors (e.g., depth, semantics, HDMaps) facilitate photorealism but lack the structural detail required for consistent guidance. In this work, we present Driving with DINO (DwD), a novel framework that leverages Vision Foundation Module (VFM) features as a unified bridge between the simulation and real-world domains. We first identify that these features encode a spectrum of information, from high-level semantics to fine-grained structure. To effectively utilize this, we employ Principal Subspace Projection to discard the high-frequency elements responsible for "texture baking," while concurrently introducing Random Channel Tail Drop to mitigate the structural loss inherent in rigid dimensionality reduction, thereby reconciling realism with control consistency. Furthermore, to fully leverage DINOv3's high-resolution capabilities for enhancing control precision, we introduce a learnable Spatial Alignment Module that adapts these high-resolution features to the diffusion backbone. Finally, we propose a Causal Temporal Aggregator employing causal convolutions to explicitly preserve historical motion context when integrating frame-wise DINO features, which effectively mitigates motion blur and guarantees temporal stability. papers.title: DriveVLA-M0: Failure-Aware Memory Augmentation for Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Zebin Xing, Yupeng Zheng, Qiang Chen, Linbo Wang, Yichen Zhang, Pengxuan Yang, Junli Wang, Deheng Qian
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving by enabling unified reasoning across perception, language, and planning. However, existing approaches lack mechanisms to exploit past failures or adapt to distribution shifts, causing the model to persistently underperform on similar scenarios where it has previously failed. In this paper, we propose DriveVLA-M0, a retrieval-augmented VLA with failure-aware latent memory. We construct a latent memory pool that stores failure cases along with their structure scene representations and expert trajectory labels, and design a dedicated Retrieve Model that decouples static road structure and dynamic agent interactions to enable structurally grounded retrieval. At inference time, retrieved cases are injected into the model via a lightweight decoupled LoRA-based test-time training (TTT) mechanism, allowing targeted and scenario-specific correction without modifying the backbone. Extensive experiments on NAVSIMv1 and NAVSIMv2 benchmark demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms prior methods, achieving 94.1 PDMS on Navtest and 47.0 EPDMS on Navhard with only 26.44 ms TTT backward latency overhead. Furthermore, we show that DriveVLA-M0 scales effectively with additional memory, enabling training-free performance gains through memory expansion. The code is available at https://github.com/ZebinX/DriveVLA-M0.

papers.title: Dream-Tac: A Unified Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Yunfan Lou, Yifan Ye, Yankai Fu, Jun Cen, Xiaowei Chi, Yaoxu Lyu, Peidong Jia, Sirui Han
papers.abstract: World action models inherit the predictive capability of world models, enabling action generation to be guided by anticipated future observations. However, they rely primarily on vision and often fail in contact-rich manipulation, where critical cues arise from physical interaction. In this paper, we propose Dream-Tac, a unified Tactile-World Action Model that jointly models actions, future visual observations, and tactile dynamics. Specifically, Dream-Tac introduces (i) contact-gated visuotactile fusion to selectively integrate tactile signals and (ii) a contact-aware attention bias to better regulate cross-modal interactions during manipulation. To support real-time deployment, we further design a dual-level acceleration strategy, reformulating the contact-aware bias to preserve the fused attention path during training and introducing cache-based diffusion acceleration at inference, achieving up to 2.9$\times$ faster training and 1.8$\times$ faster inference. Across six contact-rich manipulation tasks, Dream-Tac improves action accuracy by 31.7\% on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of unified visuotactile world modeling.Code is available at https://github.com/LYFCLOUDFAN/Dream-Tac.

papers.title: Doc2DT: An LLM-driven knowledge graph abstraction framework for digital twin generation from unstructured engineering documents
papers.authors: Yongho Lee, Sol Choi, Sang Won Lee
papers.abstract: Engineering documents contain substantial knowledge about the structure, behavior, and operation of physical systems, yet this knowledge is typically expressed in heterogeneous human-readable forms that are difficult to directly reuse in computational engineering workflows. As a result, the development of digital twins often relies on domain-specific modeling procedures and extensive manual engineering effort, limiting the reuse of generation methodologies across different systems. To address this challenge, this paper proposes Doc2DT, an LLM-driven knowledge graph abstraction framework that transforms unstructured engineering documents into reusable digital twin representations through a unified abstraction process. The framework converts document-level engineering information into structured digital representations and reformulates them as graph-based abstract models that explicitly capture engineering knowledge in a machine-interpretable form. The resulting abstraction serves as the foundation for digital twin generation and system integration. The proposed framework is evaluated through industrial robot case studies in which engineering documents are transformed into validated digital representations and deployed as operational digital twins. Additional robot casesfurther demonstrate that the same abstraction methodology can be retained despite differences in geometry, document structure, and local ambiguity. The results support the effectiveness, generality, and scalability of the proposed abstraction-centered approach within the articulated robot domain and indicate a broader pathway toward reusable digital twin generation from heterogeneous engineering documents.

papers.title: DobotTrack: Target-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Learning for Embodied Person Tracking
papers.authors: Shengjun Deng, Yinghan Zhang, Chengrui Wei, Liu Liang, Songyuan Liu, Pengkun Zheng, Yajun Zheng, Ying Zhang, et al.
papers.abstract: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.

papers.title: DexDICE: Reconciling Safety and Performance via Dual-Expert Offline Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Seokin Seo, Sung Kuk Shyn, Minji Seo, Yisoo Lee, Jongmin Lee, Hongseok Yang, Kee-Eung Kim
papers.abstract: Ensuring high returns while providing strong safety guarantees in offline imitation learning (IL) is a fundamental challenge: existing approaches either rely on explicitly specified cost functions, which are difficult to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or require expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are often too costly to collect. We introduce dual-expert imitation learning, which leverages two complementary data sources: (i) safety-compliant demonstrations that faithfully follow safety guidelines but may be suboptimal, and (ii) performance-oriented demonstrations that achieve high returns but may violate safety guidelines. To address this problem, we propose DexDICE (Dual-expert offline imitation learning via stationary DIstribution Correction Estimation). Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, enabling agents to exploit high-return behaviors while remaining within safety-compliant regions. We prove that the ideal solution satisfying this constraint exactly has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability. We evaluate DexDICE on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and validate it on a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained directly from human teleoperation demonstrations, where it substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.

papers.title: Deep learning–based object detection for automated classification of ripe and unripe tomatoes in field conditions
papers.authors: Leila Hassanzadeh, Razieh Pourdarbani, Sajad Sabzi, Omid Daliran, José Miguel Molina‐Martínez, Ginés Garcı́a-Mateos, Alberto García-Berná
papers.abstract: Accurate detection of tomatoes at different ripening stages from close-range remote sensing imagery acquired under real field conditions is a key enabler for yield estimation, harvest scheduling, and selective robotic picking in precision agriculture. However, achieving reliable performance is challenging due to occlusions, variable illumination, dense foliage, and the limited size of domain-specific datasets typically available to small farms and research teams. In this work, we present a controlled comparative study between two representative object detection paradigms, Faster R-CNN with a ResNet-50 FPN backbone (two-stage) and YOLO26s (single-stage), on a curated dataset of 367 high-resolution images acquired in a commercial cherry-tomato greenhouse under natural illumination, containing more than 8,900 manually annotated tomatoes across three classes: blossom, premature, and ripe. Both models were trained for 100 epochs under a controlled protocol sharing the same data, stratified 70/15/15 split complemented by 5-fold cross-validation, and evaluated using COCO-style AP/AR together with per-class precision–recall and ROC analyses. YOLO26s achieved a macro-average AP of 0.741 and ROC AUC of 0.954 on the held-out test split, substantially outperforming Faster R-CNN (macro AP 0.241; ROC AUC 0.836), particularly under stricter localization thresholds, and qualitative examples confirm that localization rather than classification is the main bottleneck of Faster R-CNN. These results provide actionable guidelines for deploying detectors on small agricultural remote sensing datasets in fixed monitoring stations and on ground or aerial autonomous platforms, where tighter bounding boxes and a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off are decisive for reliable operation.

papers.title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
papers.authors: Dingkun Wei, Zehong Shen, Huaijin Pi, Xueyang Wang, Xing Zhu, Hujun Bao, Yujun Shen, Xiaowei Zhou
papers.abstract: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. papers.title: Continuous Versus Discrete Tactile Representations for Vision-Language-Action Avocado Sorting
papers.authors: Ran Yang, Yuhao Lei, Li Yang, Yiming Feng
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically have no direct channel for non-visual physical properties, such as tactile ripeness: such evidence is either dropped entirely or folded into the policy as a discrete signal, a classifier output substituted into a text prompt. The latter reuses the language channel VLA models are pretrained on, but compresses a spatially structured deformation field into a low-bandwidth categorical cue represented by only a few language tokens. We investigate how the pathway used to incorporate tactile evidence affects contact-rich manipulation. Using robotic avocado ripeness sorting as a testbed, where tactile deformation cues are inaccessible to vision, we compare three conditions: a vision-only pi0 baseline with no tactile signal, discrete text-prompt conditioning on a separately trained tactile classifier, and continuous fusion, where GelSight tactile images are encoded via a pretrained DINOv2 encoder and concatenated with visual embeddings prior to the pi0 backbone, without added cross-modal attention. In a small-scale evaluation on 10 held-out avocados unseen during demonstration collection, with each specimen tested twice per method, continuous fusion reaches a 95% sorting success rate, versus 80% for discrete text-prompt conditioning and 70% with no tactile signal, at only 7.7% inference overhead over the vision-only baseline; the discrete classifier matches the specimen label in all 20 of its robot trials. The central observation is that even a correct tactile category can fail to control a pretrained action policy when communicated only through a prompt.
