papers.title: Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists
papers.authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck
papers.abstract: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI. papers.title: CoT4AD: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Explicit Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Zhaohui Wang, Tengbo Yu, Hao Tang
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently attracted growing attention in end-to-end autonomous driving for their strong reasoning capabilities and rich world knowledge. However, existing VLAs often suffer from limited numerical reasoning ability and overly simplified input-output mappings, which hinder their performance in complex driving scenarios requiring step-by-step causal reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose CoT4AD, a novel VLA framework that introduces Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning for autonomous driving to enhance both numerical and causal reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). CoT4AD integrates visual observations and language instructions to perform semantic reasoning, scene understanding, and trajectory planning. During training, it explicitly models a perception-question-prediction-action CoT to align the reasoning space with the action space across multiple driving tasks. During inference, it performs implicit CoT reasoning to enable consistent numerical reasoning and robust decision-making in dynamic environments. Extensive experiments on both real-world and simulated benchmarks, including nuScenes and Bench2Drive, demonstrate that CoT4AD achieves state-of-the-art performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluations. papers.title: Capturability-Aware Footstep Planning in Cluttered Environments: A Recursively Feasible Sequential MPC on Axis-Aligned Safe Corridors
papers.authors: Athanasios Kyriakopoulos, Shubham S. Kumbhar, Kunal S. Narkhede, Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Ioannis Poulakakis
papers.abstract: A fundamental aspect of humanoid footstep planning is to jointly guarantee obstacle avoidance and locomotion stability. This paper presents a capturability-aware sequential Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework for Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP)-based humanoid footstep planning in the presence of obstacles. The proposed method combines obstacle avoidance with capturability constraints through safe corridors constructed as sequences of intersecting rectangles, yielding a sequential MPC framework with recursive feasibility guarantees for the LIP-based planning layer. The planner autonomously adapts to constrained scenarios, switching to in-place walking when obstructions---such as doors assumed to be open during planning but unexpectedly found to be closed during execution---block forward motion. Performance is largely independent of the prediction horizon, allowing high success rates while keeping the computational cost low. The approach is validated in high-fidelity simulations with the humanoid robot Digit, demonstrating a practical solution for capturable humanoid footstep planning in cluttered environments.

papers.title: Can LLMs Debug Robots by Editing Their Weights?
papers.authors: Jusheng Zhang, Keze Wang, Liang Lin
papers.abstract: A language model can repair a robot policy's lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows. We bring weight-space programming to robot foundation policies: GPT-6 Astra reads weights and uses a CPU workspace and budgeted simulator feedback, without gradient updates or new demonstrations. Three independent sessions on $π_{0.5}$ all improve success on 765 held-out paraphrases; the best raises success from 86.3\% to 92.0\% (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired $p=1.31\times10^{-10}$). Among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens, success rises from 74.3\% to 87.5\%; the other 430 episodes have zero outcome changes. Matched random-direction edits do not help. Full replacement using the editor's own lexicon explains much of the gain but produces more regressions; its direct difference from the editor is not significant at 0.05. Across 13 further robot sessions, the editor declines 12 candidates; the sole retained edit does not show a significant held-out gain. Separately, benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0\% to 48.6\%, while the evaluated VLA's aggregate rate is unchanged. The evidence supports precise lexical repair, not general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.

papers.title: CARA: Concept-Aware Risk Attention for Interpretable Collision Anticipation
papers.authors: Zhishan Tao, Ruoyu Wang, Yucheng Wu, Enjun Du, Yilei Yuan, Sherwin Ho, Y W Su, Jinbo Su
papers.abstract: Collision anticipation in autonomous driving requires not only accurate early warnings but also interpretable reasoning about what risk factors are being tracked and how risk evolves over time. Existing methods fall short in this regard: feature-driven models are opaque, post-hoc explanations often lack fidelity, and concept-based methods are mostly designed for static recognition rather than dynamic driving scenes. We propose CARA (Concept-Aware Risk Attention), an intrinsically interpretable spatio-temporal framework for collision anticipation. CARA derives domain-grounded risk concepts from accident narratives, aligns them with video frames via vision-language similarity, and organizes them into evolving concept trajectories. These trajectories provide explicit risk evidence that guides spatial attention, temporal attention, and anticipation, allowing semantic concepts to directly influence both where the model attends and how it predicts risk over time. By treating semantic risk factors as dynamic intermediate evidence rather than auxiliary post-hoc explanations, CARA tightly couples interpretability with the predictive process. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks show that CARA consistently improves anticipation accuracy and warning earliness over strong baselines, while providing sparse and semantically grounded concept evidence.

papers.title: Bioprinted aquatic plant-inspired soft machines for underwater environmental sensing
papers.authors: Isabella Fiorello, Israel Kellersztein, Beatriz Arsuffi, Frederike Klimm, Barbara Mazzolai, Thomas Speck, Chiara Daraio
papers.abstract: Abstract Aquatic plants combine porous, compliant stems with distributed leaves that interact with complex underwater environments, but these design principles remain unexplored in soft robotics. Here we translate the architecture and biomechanics of the submerged macrophyte Myriophyllum mattogrossense into bioprinted aquatic plant-inspired soft machines. High-resolution photon-based bioprinting produced wheel-like porous hydrogel stems with approximately 38% lower flexural rigidity than solid controls (15.6±2.1 versus 25.1±2.8 N mm²), enabling large deformations under external loading. We fabricated leaf-like structures using two cellulose-based hydrogel systems. Sodium alginate-hydroxyethyl cellulose hydrogels containing Chlamydomonas reinhardtii showed progressive greening and chlorophyll autofluorescence during culture. Nanocellulose-based poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) hydrogels underwent reversible shape changes in response to temperature and salinity, with curvature increasing 6.5-fold and 4-fold, respectively. Integrating these components produced an artificial aquatic plant-like machine that remained stable underwater while retaining the mechanical and responsive properties of its stem and leaf modules. These results establish aquatic plant architecture as a source of design principles for modular biohybrid soft machines and provide a foundation for underwater environmental sensing. This responsive platform offers a route towards adaptive underwater devices for environmental monitoring, ecological research and future biohybrid robotic applications across diverse, dynamic aquatic ecosystems.

papers.title: Beyond Waypoints: A Trajectory-Centric Waypointing Paradigm for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.authors: Haoxiang Shi, Xiang Deng, Haoyu Zhang, Qiaohui Chu, Yaowei Wang, Liqiang Nie
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires agents to follow natural-language instructions while navigating in real-world-like environments. Most VLN-CE approach\-es adopt a three-stage framework: a waypoint predictor proposes navigable waypoints, and a navigator selects the best waypoint, with a low-level controller executing the movement to it. However, this decoupled paradigm often leads to unreachable waypoints or inconsistencies between planning and control. In this work, instead of predicting isolated waypoints, we introduce a novel paradigm called Trajectory Waypoint, which grounds each candidate waypoint in an executable trajectory. To realize this, we design a Trajectory Waypoint Predictor formulated as a TSDF-guided diffusion policy, which steers trajectory generation away from obstacles, inherently ensuring the reachability of the predicted waypoints. We further propose a trajectory-enhanced navigator that injects the associated trajectory as additional information for planning, enabling strict consistency between high-level semantic decisions and low-level execution. Extensive experiments on the VLN-CE benchmark show that our Trajectory Waypoint paradigm achieves superior performance over the baselines.

papers.title: Beyond Frame-Level Accuracy: Analyzing Video-Level Stability in Transformer-Based Deepfake Forensics
papers.authors: Syed Azmul Hasan, Mowmita Pervin Hera, Afroza Lona Mim, M M Jihad Hossain, Hazrat Ali, Mohammad Farhad Bulbul
papers.abstract: Deepfake videos generated by advanced generative models pose serious threats to digital security, misinformation control, and media forensics. Although numerous detection methods have been proposed, their reported performances are often based on heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, inconsistent data splits, and model-specific training protocols, hindering fair architectural comparison. This work presents a controlled and reproducible comparative study of convolutional neural networks (ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0) and a transformer-based architecture (ViT-B/16) within a unified, face-centric deepfake detection framework. All models are trained using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization settings, and data splits on Celeb-DF v2 and FaceForensics++, and results are validated across three independent random seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals. Experimental results show that while CNN-based models perform competitively at the frame level, their performance degrades after video-level aggregation. In contrast, ViT-B/16 demonstrates more stable video-level performance, achieving 92.8\% [95\% CI: 91.7--94.0] video-level accuracy and an AUC of 0.950 [95\% CI: 0.934--0.964] on Celeb-DF v2 (3-seed bootstrapped). Cross-dataset evaluation across the same three random seeds reveals a large, asymmetric generalization gap (AUC 0.79 FF++$\rightarrow$Celeb-DF vs. 0.64 Celeb-DF$\rightarrow$FF++), indicating that in-domain video-level stability does not transfer to unseen manipulation domains. These findings indicate that global self-attention improves robustness and video-level stability for deepfake detection within a given data domain, while highlighting the need for further work on cross-domain generalization.

papers.title: BATCH: Behavior Alignment for Cross-Embodiment Learning from Humans
papers.authors: Zeyi Liu, Shuran Song
papers.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. We further introduce two complementary training objectives that leverage these correspondences within an autoregressive videoaction diffusion model: behavior-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer. On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations compared with training on unaligned data and prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective. Our results demonstrate that explicit behavior alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies.

papers.abstract: Snake robots can leverage their hyper-redundant morphology for both locomotion and manipulation through distributed body contact but whole-body loco-manipulation is particularly challenging since the entire body serves simultaneously as propulsive mechanism and manipulation tool Prior work on wheeled legged and snake robot platforms has decoupled these functions through dedicated appendages body segmentation or grippers We present closed-loop loco-manipulation with our snake robot COBRA without this distinction such that any part of the body may make contact We develop a contact-implicit dynamic model unifying robot-ground robot-object and object-ground interactions within a Moreau-Jean time-stepping framework and formulate a trajectory optimization over the full-order dynamics guided by a geometric planner and nominal proportional controller to autonomously push an object to a goal location during sidewinding We validate the planner and controller on hardware across varied configurations and present simulation results for a simplified trajectory optimization that resolves robot-object and object-ground contacts

papers.title: Augmentron: Scalable Multi-View Visual Augmentation for Robot Learning
papers.authors: Tanay Tandon, Aseem Doriwala, Jade Choghari, Catherine Weaver, Pragna Mannam
papers.abstract: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive to environmental features that are unrelated to the task. Existing generative augmentation methods can introduce visual diversity, but processing every frame and camera view independently is computationally expensive and may produce inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps. We introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses. This produces temporally and multi-view consistent environ- ment and workspace variations while preserving the robot, task objects, actions, and annotations. Across three physical manipulation tasks, replacing half of the real world training dataset with Augmentron data improves model success across three tasks for both in out-of-distribution distractor objects, and out-of-distribution workspace variation evaluations. In a separate comparison against alternate augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions. The results show that introducing augmented data to a data training recipe can help policies generalize to dynamic real-world settings.

papers.title: Agibot: An Open-Source Modular Swerve-Drive Robot Platform for Agricultural Robotics Research and Education
papers.authors: Moeen Ul Islam, Bishal Adhikari, Kori Edwards, Lorien Harvey, J. Alex Thomasson, Dong Chen
papers.abstract: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. By combining affordability, modularity, open-source accessibility, configurable manipulation, and end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify autonomy, Agibot provides a practical platform for agricultural robotics research, technology development, and workforce training.

papers.title: AeroGuide: Grounded Vision-Language Navigation in Aerial Environments
papers.authors: Abhinav Upadhyay, Siddharth Singh, Satvik Srivastava, Tanya Khanna, Ashutosh Pandey, Shashi Shekhar Jha
papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) requires a UAV to follow natural language instructions from visual observations. Aerial VLN is more challenging than ground-level VLN because UAV observations cover large outdoor areas, landmarks often occupy only a small part of the image, and navigation requires complex spatial reasoning. General-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) often struggle to identify instruction-relevant visual evidence from such dense aerial observations. We propose AeroGuide, a grounded aerial VLN framework built on Qwen3-VL. AeroGuide introduces Navigation-conditioned Visual Token Routing (NVTR), which selects instruction-relevant visual tokens conditioned on the current observation, UAV pose, and temporal landmark memory. AeroGuide maintains an egocentric temporal landmark memory that retains compact landmark evidence rather than full historical frames. The model is trained through multiple phases, including supervised learning, reasoning distillation, and simulator-based policy optimization, to improve grounded action prediction and closed-loop navigation. On the OpenFly benchmark, AeroGuide improves navigation success rate from 34.3% to 45.1%, a 31.5% relative improvement over the best-performing prior baseline. Ablation studies show that explicit visual grounding and compact temporal memory are key contributors to this improvement, demonstrating the effectiveness of grounded navigation for aerial VLN. Project page is available at https://aeroguide-frontend-iota.vercel.app/.

Equipped with multiple sensors and various electronic devices, the robot is designed to detect enemy presence, capture camera footage, and live-stream data to authorized personnel. This robot enables armed forces to proficiently monitor isolated areas and respond immediately to potential threats. Human risk is reduced by using this type of robot surveillance system. Deploying robots in high-risk isolated areas minimizes personnel exposure to potential threats while maintaining effective surveillance. The use of autonomous technology increases operational efficiency by enabling continuous surveillance without requiring constant human intervention. By combining cutting-edge embedded technology, real-time monitoring, and remote operability, this robot vehicle delivers a consistent and effective solution for border or boundary security. Integrating advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), embedded systems, and very large-scale integration (VLSI), will significantly enhance the capabilities and efficiency of the robot in armed forces. This robot provides not only a human-free system but also an efficient smart system to address military challenges.

papers.title: Adaptive dual-programming magnetic soft robot with lifelike behavior
papers.authors: Yanchen Ye, Can Xu, Sen Wang, Weijia Li, Rongye Wu, Hao Wu, Neng Xia, TianYe Yang
papers.abstract: Magnetic soft robots with embodied intelligence of multimodal motions, environmental perception, and functional decoupling depend on ingenious material arrangement and programmable morphing information introduction. While some efforts have been made, achieving lifelike behaviors for soft robots in system-level strategy remains a notable challenge. Here, we present dual-programming hydrogel-based soft robots (DHSRs) that couple magnetic and anisotropic programming through the spatial arrangement of patterned magnetic skeletons into responsive and structural hydrogel bodies. These DHSRs exhibit programmable exquisite and multicurved structures in three-dimensional (3D) space, environment-adaptive deformation behaviors proved by switching from random jumping on land to regular swimming in water of a fish-like soft robot, and further locomotion-function decoupling capabilities of region-selective cargo delivery in an integrated "locomotion-perception-action" workflow. Our strategy in biomedical potential is exemplified by a ring-like pH-responsive DHSR for gastric ulcer therapy, which integrates multimodal locomotion (rolling, tumbling, and rotating), adaptive matching, and microneedle-mediated penetration. By collaborating with a capsule endoscopy system, we explore the possibility of a wireless and painless diagnostic-therapeutic platform in a pig model. This strategy endows the robot with perception and multitask execution capabilities, highlighting a promising route for the intelligent evolution of soft robots across diverse application domains.

papers.title: ActPrune: Action-Grounded Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Sungwon Moon, Minji Kim, Hyemin Boo, Daeun Song, Jiyoung Lee
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.

papers.title: ActDistill: General Action-Guided Self-Derived Distillation for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Wencheng Ye, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown impressive flexibility and generalization, yet their deployment in robotic manipulation remains limited by heavy computational overhead and inference latency. In this work, we present ActDistill, a general action-guided self-derived distillation framework that transfers the action prediction capability of any existing VLA model to a lightweight counterpart. Unlike previous efficiency strategies that primarily emphasize vision-language correlations, ActDistill leverages action priors to guide knowledge transfer and model compression, achieving action-oriented efficiency for VLA models. Specifically, we employ a well-trained VLA model as the teacher and introduce a graph-structured encapsulation strategy to explicitly model the hierarchical evolution of action prediction. The student model, derived from the graph-encapsulated teacher, is further equipped with a dynamic router that adaptively selects computation paths based on action prediction demands, guided by hierarchical graph-informed supervision to ensure smooth and efficient evolution. During inference, graph-related auxiliary components are removed, allowing the student to execute only dynamically routed layers and predict high-precision actions with minimal computation and latency. Experiments on embodied benchmarks demonstrate that ActDistill achieves comparable or superior performance to full-scale VLA models while reducing computation by over 50% with up to 1.67 times speedup, thereby establishing a general paradigm toward efficient embodied intelligence.

papers.title: ATLAS: A Multi-Procedure Benchmark and Context-Aware Model for Surgical Anatomy Segmentation
papers.authors: Ronald L. P. D. de Jong, Tim J. M. Jaspers, Raf A. H. Vervoort, Aron F. H. A. Bakker, Anna L. Dijk, Yiping Li, Jip L. Tolenaar, Jelle P. Ruurda, et al.
papers.abstract: Recognizing anatomical structures during minimally invasive surgery (MIS) could support intraoperative navigation and improve patient safety, but progress is limited by small, single-procedure datasets and by segmentation methods developed for natural scenes. This work addresses both limitations through a new dataset and model. First, we introduce ATLAS-120k, a clip-level semantic segmentation dataset of 121,018 annotated frames from 100 surgical videos, covering 14 laparoscopic and robot-assisted procedures and 41 classes. Annotations were created with a pipeline that combines manual labeling, tracker-based propagation, and review by surgeons. Second, we propose ATLAS (Anatomy Recognition with Context Learning using Foundation Representations), a video semantic segmentation model for surgical anatomy recognition. ATLAS builds on in-domain foundation-model embeddings and adds context queries for the procedure and surgical phase, together with query propagation between frames for short-term memory. ATLAS outperforms state-of-the-art natural-image and in-domain foundation models in both segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency, achieving a Dice score of 0.70 with ViT-L while running in real time at 76.2 FPS. Ablations show that the context queries improve accuracy and that query propagation improves temporal consistency. ATLAS also generalizes well, matching a dedicated model zero-shot on CholecSeg8k and improving phase recognition on AutoLaparo over SurgeNet initialization. papers.title: ARFlow: Real-time Human Action-Reaction Synthesis with Reprojection Guidance
papers.authors: Wentao Jiang, Jingya Wang, Kaiyang Ji, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang, Ye Shi
papers.abstract: Human action-reaction synthesis, a fundamental challenge in modeling causal human interactions, plays a critical role in applications ranging from virtual reality to social robotics. While diffusion-based models have demonstrated promising performance, they exhibit two key limitations for interaction synthesis: reliance on complex noise-to-reaction generators with intricate conditional mechanisms, and frequent physical violations in generated motions. To address these issues, we propose Action-Reaction Flow Matching (ARFlow), a novel framework that establishes direct action-to-reaction mappings, eliminating the need for complex conditional mechanisms. Our approach introduces a physical guidance mechanism specifically designed for Flow Matching (FM) that effectively prevents body penetration artifacts during sampling. Moreover, we discover the bias of traditional flow matching sampling algorithm and employ a reprojection method to revise the sampling direction of FM. To further enhance the reaction diversity, we incorporate randomness into the sampling process. Extensive experiments on NTU120, Chi3D and InterHuman datasets demonstrate that ARFlow not only outperforms existing methods in terms of Fréchet Inception Distance and motion diversity but also significantly reduces body collisions, as measured by our new Intersection Volume and Intersection Frequency metrics.

papers.title: AI, Analytics, and Action Execution in Physical AI for Healthcare
papers.authors: Nilmini Wickramasinghe
papers.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), advanced analytics, and autonomous action execution is driving the emergence of Physical AI as a transformative paradigm in healthcare. Unlike conventional digital AI systems that primarily generate predictions or recommendations, Physical AI integrates intelligent reasoning with embodied systems capable of perceiving, deciding, and acting within real-world clinical environments. These systems combine multimodal sensing, machine learning, robotics, edge computing, and adaptive control mechanisms to enable timely, context-aware, and safe interventions across healthcare settings. This chapter examines how AI, analytics, and action execution collectively underpin the next generation of intelligent healthcare systems. The chapter first explores the foundational AI methods that power Physical AI, including computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, generative AI, and foundation models, highlighting their role in interpreting complex clinical data and supporting autonomous decision-making. It then discusses the importance of analytics pipelines that transform continuous streams of physiological, environmental, imaging, and operational data into actionable insights for patient monitoring, risk prediction, workflow optimization, and precision care. Particular attention is given to real-time analytics at the edge, federated intelligence, and explainable AI approaches necessary for high-stakes healthcare environments. A central focus of the chapter is action execution; the capability of intelligent systems to move beyond recommendations and perform physical or semi-autonomous tasks. Examples include robotic surgery, automated medication dispensing, rehabilitation exoskeletons, smart hospital logistics, assistive robots for aged care, and responsive devices for acute and home-based care. The chapter evaluates how closed-loop systems that connect sensing, analytics, and autonomous action can improve efficiency, reduce clinician burden, enhance patient safety, and personalize interventions. The chapter also addresses critical implementation challenges, including trust, safety assurance, human–AI collaboration, interoperability, cybersecurity, regulatory governance, ethical accountability, and workforce readiness. It argues that successful adoption requires designing systems that augment rather than replace clinicians, while maintaining transparency and patient-centered care. By synthesizing technological advances and healthcare applications, this chapter presents Physical AI as a major step toward intelligent, adaptive, and operational healthcare ecosystems. The integration of AI, analytics, and action execution has the potential to revolutionize clinical decision-making and patient care delivery across hospitals, community settings, and future digitally enabled health systems.

papers.title: AI involvement scenarios and perceived responsibility attribution in a human–AI legal decision vignette: associations with psychological ownership and sense of control
papers.authors: Feihu Liu, Li Li
papers.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in consequential decisions, including legal and administrative judgments. When an AI-assisted decision has an adverse outcome, observers may find it difficult to determine how responsibility should be attributed to the human and AI actors. Objective This randomized vignette experiment examined perceived responsibility attribution across three bundled AI-assisted legal-decision scenarios. The scenarios varied AI functionality, human decision authority, and opportunities to intervene together. Post-vignette psychological ownership and perceived control were examined as condition-proximal perceptions associated with responsibility judgments. Methods Three hundred adults were retained for analysis (100 per condition). Each participant read one vignette describing an already completed legal decision and assessed the perceived responsibility of a fictional human reviewer and an AI system after an adverse outcome. Participants did not make a sentencing decision or interact with a functioning AI system. Randomized group contrasts were the principal comparisons. Secondary, exploratory mediation models used two indicator variables, with the low-AI scenario as the reference; post-vignette AI trust was excluded from the primary exploratory specification. Parallel and reverse-order models were examined as sensitivity analyses. Results The manipulation check differed across conditions, F (2, 297) = 1065.77, p < 0.001, η 2 = 0.878. Perceived human responsibility declined from the low- to the moderate- and high-AI scenarios, whereas perceived AI responsibility increased. The randomized mean differences in perceived human responsibility were −1.12 (moderate versus low) and −1.69 (high versus low). Exploratory indirect associations were negative via psychological ownership ( B = −0.385 and −0.713), perceived control ( B = −0.146 and −0.168), and the proposed ownership-to-control sequence ( B = −0.190 and −0.353), respectively; corresponding confidence intervals are reported in the Results. The indirect-effect intervals were calculated using delta-method approximations. Conclusion The randomized scenario comparisons showed differences in perceived responsibility attribution. Because the scenarios jointly varied multiple features, these findings do not isolate the causal effects of AI functionality, human authority, or opportunities to intervene. Ownership and control ratings partly reflected information supplied in the vignettes and therefore cannot establish distinct causal mediating mechanisms or their temporal sequence.

papers.title: AI Training Manager: Bounded Closed-Loop Control of Adaptive Training Recipes
papers.authors: Anjali Rao, Nikhil Kamalkumar Advani
papers.abstract: We present the AI Training Manager, a bounded LLM-based metacognitive monitoring-and-control layer for machine-learning training. The Manager asynchronously observes structured telemetry from an active training run, assesses the current training regime, and selects adaptive interventions through a constrained, deterministically verified action interface. We evaluate the feasibility of this architecture using deliberately induced, interpretable failure modes in supervised and reinforcement learning tasks. For supervised learning, we induce a multi-objective overfitting failure in a GPT-2-style model trained on TinyStories. The Manager prevents the resulting late-run validation collapse, reducing final validation loss by 54.3% relative to the same stressed recipe. For reinforcement learning, we study robotic reaching under opposing multifactor stress regimes. In a conservative regime, the Manager raises final deterministic safe success from 0.413 to 0.705. In an aggressive regime, it raises safe success from 0.121 to 0.764. The same Manager instructions and action surface are used in both regimes. These results suggest that bounded LLM reasoning can provide a practical metacognitive control layer over ongoing learning processes.

papers.title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
papers.authors: Chaoran Li, Yukun Li, Zeyuan Zhao, Shao Zhang, Xihuai Wang, Ying Wen
papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.

papers.title: A wearable input/output interface learns personalized models of haptic perception
papers.authors: Wen Li, E. Magnus Adams, Zijie Xu, Jiawen Yao, Aybala Esmer, Xiaoyue Ni, Bozhi Tian, Pedro Lopes
papers.abstract: Wearable haptic interfaces deliver physical stimuli to the skin, yet perceived locations vary widely across users and diverge from actuator locations, particularly for emergent tactile-feedback techniques. We developed a wearable haptic input/output (I/O) device integrating a 36-channel electrotactile array with capacitive touch sensing, enabling stimulation and user-reported percept locations to be registered within the same body-referenced coordinate frame. In 24 participants, the device revealed electrotactile and referred-thermal perceptual maps with notable interparticipant variability. Despite this variability, both modalities retained electrode-pair-specific spatial structure across participants. Tactile and thermal percepts also showed spatial correspondence, whose strength varied across participants. These findings motivated our human-in-the-loop calibration framework, which adapts a forward-prediction strategy to individual users and generates personalized perceptual models. These models enabled inverse rendering by selecting stimulation patterns predicted to generate a target percept for a specific user. Using these models, we demonstrate personalized haptic rendering in haptic-guided robot teleoperation, visual-to-haptic sensory substitution, interpersonal haptic communication, and virtual reality (VR). Together, this platform provides a route toward adaptive haptic interfaces that measure, model, and render according to each user's perception.

papers.title: A review of reinforcement learning-based decision-making for autonomous driving in risk scenarios
papers.authors: Yi Xie, Jianyuan Guo, Yong Qin, Chenxu Li
papers.abstract: Purpose Risk scenarios are a primary source of decision failures in autonomous driving. This study aims to systematically review reinforcement learning–based decision-making in such scenarios, analyze key challenges and future research directions and provide theoretical and methodological support for the development of safe and reliable autonomous driving systems. Design/methodology/approach This study analyzes the characteristics and decision-making complexity of risk scenarios, and summarizes reinforcement learning frameworks and core methods for addressing these challenges. It focuses on three representative scenario types and examines their impacts on state representation, reward design and decision-making mechanisms. To address data scarcity, recent advances in safety-critical scenario generation are reviewed, comparing data-driven, adversarial and knowledge-based approaches and summarizing their key features and development trends. Findings The results show that different risk scenarios require distinct environment modeling and decision-making mechanisms, placing higher demands on state representation, reward design and policy learning in reinforcement learning. Although safety-critical scenario generation methods help mitigate data scarcity, trade-offs among realism, diversity and controllability remain. Key challenges persist in dynamic risk modeling, human–vehicle interaction and safety verification and assurance. Originality/value This study systematically integrates existing research on reinforcement learning for autonomous driving decision-making from the perspective of risk scenarios, and establishes a comprehensive analytical framework covering scenario modeling, decision-making methods and data generation. It further provides an in-depth discussion of emerging issues, offering valuable insights and directions for future research.

papers.title: A Unified Inertial Encoder for Human and Humanoid Motion
papers.authors: Yutian Chen, Shibo Zhao, Rocky Duan, Karen Liu, Carmelo Sferrazza, Guanya Shi, Yuheng Qiu, Koushil Sreenath
papers.abstract: Learning humanoid state estimation and language-grounded motion understanding from robot recordings ties training coverage to the robot's motion repertoire. Human motion datasets offer broader coverage, yet transferring this knowledge requires overcoming differences in body geometry, sensing, and physical disturbances. To enable this transfer, we propose a unified inertial encoder whose shared inertial interface uses kinematic IMU synthesis to represent human and humanoid motion at corresponding body sites. Within this common input space, joint training on human and kinematically retargeted humanoid motion combines velocity estimation and motion--text alignment with continuous-time encoding and sensor and motion randomization. The resulting model transfers zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulation, real-robot training trajectories, or fine-tuning, achieving the lowest velocity error among evaluated methods across five datasets, including 0.099m/s on real G1. Its motion-description retrieval also extends to retargeted G1 motion categories observed only in human training, demonstrating how human motion knowledge can support the generalization of humanoid inertial odometry and language-grounded motion understanding.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Physical AI from a Multimedia Perspective: Part II Cosmos Foundation Model
papers.authors: Yang Liu, Haiwei Dong, Abdulmotaleb El Saddik
papers.abstract: Physical AI aims to enable systems to perceive, reason, and act in the unstructured physical world, yet it faces bottlenecks of scarce real-world data and high deployment risks. Traditional hand-engineered simulators provide controllable environments yet struggle with scalable coverage of diverse scenes and long-tail scenarios. Cosmos addresses these challenges as a data-driven world foundation model platform, unifying generation- verification loop to form a closed-loop data flywheel for Physical AI development. This tutorial systematically introduces Cosmos's multi-modal design, core components, and practical deployment, offering a comprehensive guide for leveraging learned world models in physical system training and evaluation.

papers.title: A Survey of Self-Evolving Embodied Agents: On the Path to Real-World Physical Intelligence
papers.authors: Xiangyu Dong, Zirong Zhang, Maozhi Li, Huanhuan Ke, Xiaoguang Ma
papers.abstract: Embodied artificial intelligence is moving beyond static task execution toward agents that can continuously adapt, learn, and improve through physical interaction with the world. While recent advances in large language models, vision-language models, robotic foundation models, vision-language-action models, and world models have significantly enhanced the perception, reasoning, and action capabilities of embodied agents, most existing systems remain constrained by offline training, fixed policies, and limited post-deployment adaptability. This survey investigates self-evolving embodied agents as an emerging research agenda for advancing toward real-world physical intelligence. We define self-evolution as the capability of embodied agents to accumulate experience, detect and correct errors, update memory, policies, skills, and models, and expand their capability boundaries through long-term interaction. To make the review auditable, we specify the literature scope, inclusion criteria, evidence types, and coding rules used in the comparative tables. We first clarify the conceptual foundations of self-evolving embodied agents and distinguish them from related paradigms such as test-time adaptation, online learning, continual learning, and lifelong learning. We then propose a unified closed-loop framework consisting of perception, state representation, memory, reasoning and planning, action, feedback, reflection, and evolution. Based on this framework, we review the historical progression from classical robotics and offline embodied learning to embodied foundation models, interactive adaptation, and self-evolving agents. We further summarize key mechanisms supporting self-evolution, including data and experience acquisition, memory-centric learning, world-modeldriven prediction, feedback-based reflection, policy and skill evolution, multi-agent co-evolution, and safety-aligned updating. Finally, we discuss representative tasks, benchmarks, evaluation protocols, open challenges, and future directions. This survey argues that self-evolution is a necessary but still weakly evidenced step toward embodied agents that can safely, autonomously, and continually grow in open-ended real-world environments.

papers.title: A ROS-based Simulation Framework for Industrial Robotics Pick-and-Place Application: Integration of Vision-based Pose Estimation and 3-DOF Inverse Kinematics
papers.authors: Kamil Çetin, Duygu Danacı
papers.abstract: The efficiency of industrial automation depends heavily on the precision and reliability of robotic pick-and-place applications. This paper presents a complete simulation framework designed to develop and validate such applications in the ROS (Robot Operating System) environment. We perform a closed-form inverse kinematics analysis for the 3-degree-of-freedom OpenManipulator-X, providing the critical transformation from task-oriented Cartesian space to the manipulator's joint space. We apply this kinematic solution to the robot using an OpenCV-based image processing algorithm, enabling the robot to dynamically target a planar object position estimation. Within the ROS architecture, pose data is broadcast from our vision node and subscribed to by the inverse kinematics node, which calculates the required joint configurations. To achieve the smooth and precise motion required in industrial environments, a cubic trajectory is generated for joint space, and a PID controller is implemented to ensure the end-effector accurately grasps the target object. All simulation studies are conducted in the Gazebo environment, demonstrating a robust and integrated process from visual detection to successful manipulation.

papers.title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics
papers.authors: Kaiyuan Chen, Xinyue Zhu, Shuangyu Xie, Uksang Yoo, Thi Thu Phuong Luong, Marcus Gualtieri, Christian Juette, Liu Ren, et al.
papers.abstract: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.
